title: The Curse of the Incumbent
excerpt: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the
body: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture
Heading into yesterday’s first round of presidential voting in Brazil, the incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, was thought to be a narrow favorite
When the results came in, though, Lula was behind his challenger, Flávio Bolsonaro, 45 percent to 47 percent
The two men will compete in an October 25 runoff to determine the winner

Those surnames will likely be recognizable even to casual watchers of global elections: Lula, a leftist, has been the dominant force in Brazilian politics this century, and was president from 2003 to 2011

Bolsonaro’s father, Jair, was a right-wing president from 2019 to 2023 but was defeated by Lula in a comeback bid; Bolsonaro the elder then attempted a Trumpian autogolpe to stay in power but failed and was later convicted and sentenced to prison for it
Now it’s Lula who’s struggling with voters

He was hurt by crime concerns as well as a corruption scandal, but he’s also a very familiar figure to Brazilians—perhaps too familiar. “Brazil wants change and I am very happy with the results,” Bolsonaro fils said last night

What kind of change, though? When Donald Trump completed his own presidential comeback in the 2024 U.S. election, one common explanation was that a fundamental change had occurred in American politics, realigning demographics, parties, and policy for the long run. (As I have written recently, that claim looks shaky today .) A competing narrative, especially popular among comparative scholars, focused on a wave of anti-incumbent results in elections around the world

In this view, the results were more a rejection of Joe Biden’s administration and his vice president, Kamala Harris, than they were an embrace of Trump—and part of a broad trend of dissatisfaction among voters in many countries
The specific motivations of the global anti-incumbent wave have never been entirely obvious
They include a post-COVID hangover but also deeper running dissatisfaction with democratic systems of government
Whatever the reasons, the trend is an important shift
Parties lose power from time to time in any country with free and fair elections, but political scientists have long observed that incumbents have an electoral advantage
In the modern United States, for example, Trump’s and Biden’s single presidential terms were outliers
If voters’ default stance is to throw the bums out after only one term or a few years, parties and leaders will struggle to create lasting policy changes
This creates instability and conflict, as politicians try more extreme tactics to achieve their goals
Lula’s poor showing in the first round, at least, is a sign that the anti-incumbent wave has not receded since 2024
Indeed, politicians across the political spectrum have faced serious voter anger this year
In Hungary, a broad coalition emerged to eject the right-wing strongman Viktor Orbán, who, my colleague Isaac Stanley-Becker noted, had been viewed as un-oustable
In Denmark, the governing coalition lost seats, though Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, a centrist, was eventually able to form a new, weaker government

In Germany, Chancellor Friedrich Merz is unpopular, and his future looks precarious , as parties on both the left and the right have gained in state elections, leaving his centrist government teetering
And today, the center-left Spanish Prime Minister, Pedro Sánchez called for a November 29 snap election for Parliament, with polls showing his party trailing behind the center-right Popular Party
The power of the anti-incumbent wave is demonstrated by the fact that it now threatens to wash out some of the same parties and politicians it previously carried in
Lula’s victory in Brazil’s 2022 election was in part a testament to voters rejecting the government of the incumbent, Jair Bolsonaro
Now the same dissatisfaction could swamp Lula and elect Bolsonaro’s son
In the United Kingdom, anti-incumbent currents helped defeat a long-running Conservative government in 2024
The result was a landslide: Conservatives lost 251 seats while Labour picked up 211 and a huge majority
But Prime Minister Keir Starmer lasted just two years in office before sagging popularity led to his effective toppling by another Labour politician, Andy Burnham
In what may be a canny reading of the global mood, Burnham has rejected suggestions that he call an election before he is required to do so, in 2029
Finally, there’s Trump, who benefited from anti-incumbent sentiments in 2024 but may be burned by them in November
Voters may not have liked Biden, but now that they’ve seen Trump back in the White House, they like him even less
Among other issues, the inflation that hurt Biden (and other global incumbents) in 2024 has persisted and sometimes worsened under Trump
Midterm elections in the U.S. are usually defeats for the sitting president’s party, but many analysts now forecast a larger-than-normal Democratic victory
Trump has begged voters to act as though he is on the ballot, but that may be imprudent
Anti-incumbency is a global trend, but it can have big effects on domestic politics
In the United States, Trump treated his narrow 2024 win as a huge popular mandate
Although that was a political overreach, he has managed to radically reshape the federal government and foreign policy
In Brazil, a new Bolsonaro presidency would jerk the country back toward the right after a leftward lurch under Lula
As long as voters remain this dyspeptic, however, any new approach should be treated as fragile and fleeting

title: Hegseth’s One Percent
excerpt: Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth is again focusing his attention on junior officers and noncommissioned officers
body: Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth is again focusing his attention on junior officers and noncommissioned officers

In a speech delivered September 30 at the Marine Corps base in Quantico, Virginia, he invoked a verse he has frequently cited, Isaiah 6:8— And I heard the voice of the Lord, saying: Whom shall I send, And who will go for us? Then I said: Here am I; send me
Understandably, in these remarks he does not quote a rather more applicable previous verse: Then said I: Woe is me! For I am undone; Because I am a man of unclean lips

Isaiah volunteered for the solitary and dangerous task of reproaching a corrupt court that confused ritual with faith, filled with those who oppress the widow and the orphan, “grind the face of the poor,” and “declare their sin as Sodom, they hide it not.” He was, according to the Talmud, eventually sawed in two by the evil king Manasseh

The eighth-century B.C.E. prophet was not joining a military of well more than 1 million men and women with competitive pay, excellent lifelong benefits, and the right to board an airplane ahead of an 80-year-old grandmother

Hegseth is a ludicrous figure in many ways—the strutting sycophant who has promised a military with “no fatties, no trannies, no beardos, no weirdos”; the flaunter of push-ups that are performative but out of regs; the grown man stuck at the development level of an angry first lieutenant; the testosterone-obsessed infantry officer who, unlike most of his peers, never managed to earn a Ranger tab
Even so, we should take what he is saying seriously. [ Read: Pete Hegseth, idea guy ] Following the Quantico speech, Hegseth spoke to cadets at the U.S
Air Force Academy before the annual Air Force–Navy football game

In what is now his stump speech, he called them “the real one percent” of our society who have “a perspective that 99 percent of Americans do not have.” For 251 years, he said, America has required “the absolute best” to stand up and redeem the rest of us
It is not only balderdash, but dangerous balderdash

With the greatest possible respect for the work of the all-volunteer military of the past 50 years—with acknowledgment of its hardship, suffering, and loss—the fact is that the armed forces of the United States have fought the country’s most important and difficult wars not with the one percent, but with all the rest of us: the doughboys and the GIs who cheerfully or reluctantly went when called, and who yearned to get the job done, go home, and resume civilian life
George Washington’s Continentals were vital to winning American independence—but so, too, were the thousands of militiamen who harried British troops

The Civil War was won with mass armies; the American Expeditionary Force of World War I was filled by soldiers inducted through the Selective Service System, as were the armies of World War II, Korea, and Vietnam
In American history, only our lesser wars were fought exclusively with volunteers, and many of those who fought them were recent immigrants looked down upon by those who got here before them
In the fall of 1863, Abraham Lincoln contemplated conscription for the Union armies

In his cool appraisal , he noted: At the beginning of the war, and ever since, a variety of motives pressing, some in one direction and some in the other, would be presented to the mind of each man physically fit for a soldier, upon the combined effect of which motives, he would, or would not, voluntarily enter the service
Among these motives would be patriotism, political bias, ambition, personal courage, love of adventure, want of employment, and convenience, or the opposites of some of these
People enlist for all kinds of reasons, but not necessarily because they are morally, physically, or mentally the best

Moreover, the brute fact is that the challenges faced by our professional forces have been different from and smaller than those confronted by America’s previous mass militaries of short-term volunteers and conscripts

Again, with respect and gratitude to today’s American soldiers, the Iraqis, Taliban, and Iranians were lesser opponents than the Wehrmacht, the Korean People’s Army, the Chinese People’s Liberation Army, and the People’s Army of Vietnam
Against its more recent enemies, the United States has brought to bear infinitely superior weapons, an array of allies, and usually greater numbers

It is a far cry from American sailors up against Japanese heavy cruisers and German U-boats; American soldiers staring down the barrel of the 88-millimeter gun on a King Tiger tank from a much-flimsier Sherman or watching bazooka rounds bounce off a T-34; or airmen jousting with Russian-piloted MiG-15s over the Yalu River. [ Read: Pete Hegseth’s magic marker ] What is even worse than biblical illiteracy and historical ignorance from this product of Princeton and Harvard Universities is a project about which he seems to be deadly serious: the cultural isolation of the military

His speeches subtly denigrate the general officer corps and focus on the most impressionable segment of the military, those old enough to have bought into the system but young enough to be naive about its merits
What Hegseth is saying amounts to this: Y ou are better than 99 percent of your fellow Americans
You are crusaders, and they—particularly the media and the intellectuals—are not only uncomprehending of your merits but ready to subvert you

We want to select you from a specific slice of society: We want socially conservative young men and (very few) women from Liberty University and Hillsdale, not from liberal research universities and colleges
We want you to be isolated on bases from the rest of this corrupt society, which we despise, as should you
It is profoundly dangerous stuff, the antithesis of what soldiers such as George C

Marshall or Dwight Eisenhower believed, that the soldier is a citizen first, that one cannot adequately defend this society without believing in its values and its essential goodness, that an air of contempt is incompatible with a life of self-abnegation
A Hegsethian cult of military superiority over civilians is not only unwarranted, but actively dangerous
If allowed to fester, it will breed a military detached from America, poorly educated, and contemptuous of the press and all politicians save those of the Trumpian stripe
The force will be narrowly recruited, unrepresentative of a magnificently diverse country, insular, and obsessed with technical matters
It will resemble nothing so much as the Imperial German Army that led its country to disaster in World War I
That the secretary of defense, himself bearing a Crusader tattoo, begins this project by quoting a lonely man of faith is little short of blasphemy.

About Mike: In addition to having broken some of the most consequential stories of our time, Mike is also a brilliant writer and fantastically creative
On a personal level, he is also hilarious

title: The Upgrade Holdouts
excerpt: A decade ago, an Apple executive named Phil Schiller had a message for people using computers that were more than five years old. “This is really sad,” he said,
body: A decade ago, an Apple executive named Phil Schiller had a message for people using computers that were more than five years old. “This is really sad,” he said, with apparent sincerity, to scattered applause during an iPad Pro launch event

The remark was meant, seemingly, to encourage those poor souls to toss their obsolete devices aside and upgrade their way toward the future. (In other words: buy more Apple products.) That was 2016, during the era when Apple announced new products to great fanfare, the average iPhone user traded in their device about every 23 months, and releases came with promises that buyers would “never want to go back to old technology again.” Over the years, more and more Americans have begun to rethink this upgrade formula
Some of them are turning to secondhand-tech marketplaces ; others are combing eBay to pick up obsolete gadgets that remind them of a more offline time

But there exists another segment of the population that’s taken a different approach: They’ve refused to replace their devices at all. [ Read: There’s no reason to buy a new phone anymore ] Call them legacy users, or upgrade holdouts

They’ve clung to iPhones with home buttons, Bush-era computers, and headphones older than some tech CEOs, even when doing so impedes their ability to complete everyday tasks like emailing or navigation
The holdouts I spoke with don’t necessarily reject technology
Instead, they told me, they just want to use it on their own terms
Some members of this community are older and put off by the prospect of learning a new interface
Others are minimalists who appreciate the simplicity of older technology, or anti-consumerism advocates looking to retain a sense of autonomy

Many aren’t driven by any sort of principle at all besides mere practicality: When I asked Larye Parkins—the proud user of a Compaq computer released in 2007, the same year that Superbad hit the box office and Myspace dominated social media—what he would call himself, he came back with a simple reply: “I’m just cheap.” In some cases, their devices are old enough to now be on display in museums
Mike Tyran, a 66-year-old nurse, has long jammed out to ’80s glam bands on his 2003 iPod, a subsequent model of which can be found in the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History
Tyran also uses a smartphone, computer, and television that are all nearly a decade old and goes by “Old Turkey” on iFixit, a website dedicated to tech repairs
There, he dispenses and gathers tips on maintaining aging gadgets

Like many other holdouts, Tyran has no interest in contributing to e-waste heaps or shelling out five figures for gadgets with AI capabilities. “I have ‘NI’—natural intelligence,” he told me. “I’m good with that.” The common enemy of upgrade holdouts is planned obsolescence, or deliberately designing products to have short lifespans

The term was coined nearly a century ago by the real-estate broker Bernard London. “There is little demand for new goods when people make their old and worn-out things do, by keeping them longer than they should,” London wrote
Today, no industry is more closely associated with the practice than Big Tech
Take Apple, which in 2020 agreed to settle lawsuits alleging that it was secretly slowing down older iPhones

Beyond “batterygate,” the company has also long engaged in “parts pairing,” the practice of preventing certain third-party parts from working in a repaired device, and discontinued hardware service for hundreds of its products over the years
When it comes to continuing to use early smartphone models, just getting them to connect can be a problem
The 2G and 3G cellular networks they ran on have been largely phased out across North America (the latter can be found only in certain geographic enclaves)

One of those pockets is in Saint John, New Brunswick, where Gary Flanagan—among the 2.3 percent of customers still using Koodo Mobile’s “legacy” network—managed to call me from his iPhone 5S, first released in 2013
Flanagan, a 54-year-old nonprofit consultant, occasionally finds himself unable to download apps or watch YouTube videos, and his younger co-workers rib him
But for the most part, he’s content. “If it works, it works—and I still use it,” Flanagan, who also still wears a pair of Radio Shack headphones he was gifted in 1983, told me
Nathan Proctor, the right-to-repair campaign director for the U.S
Public Interest Research Group, told me that some devices are made obsolete overnight, while others die a slow death as software updates are gradually halted
In order to keep using them, holdouts must contend with constraints in their day-to-day lives
Mark Turner, the owner of a nearly 10-year-old smartphone, told me he’s prolonged buying a newer version of his hearing aids because their pairing app isn’t able to run on his device

Others, such as Kentaro Toyama, a computer scientist and University of Michigan professor who uses an AT&T flip phone, find work-arounds to navigate a world powered by QR codes—for Toyama, that means borrowing his wife’s old smartphone
Such trade-offs can be a small price to pay for maintaining a sense of control over one’s digital presence
As a freelance copywriter and editor, Josh Fredman says laptops are essential for him

But the 44-year-old has put off replacing his computers—a 16-year-old Toshiba and a 13-year-old HP model—because they serve as an oasis from today’s digital spaces, free from the constant notifications and update alerts of modern operating systems
One of Fredman’s laptops can no longer connect to the internet and has become his “art computer,” used for writing fiction and composing music
He’s replaced faulty fans and hard drives on the other laptop, and installed a gaming package from 2009 that allows him to play Solitaire without the interruption of advertisements
Keeping old hardware alive is often a communal effort
Last year, iFixit helped host several “install parties” of Linux, an open-source operating system that can breathe new life into obsolete computers, at cafés and libraries across the country
A simple search on YouTube brings up numerous how-to guides on jailbreaking Kindles in order to free older models from Amazon’s software restrictions
And a decade ago, fans of the discontinued smartwatch brand Pebble grouped together to create Rebble, a platform of web services that reinvigorated technically defunct smartwatches
Wayne Seltzer, who got his Pebble watch as a Father’s Day gift in 2015, told me he appreciates the “kindred spirits” nature of the project

Similar sentiments against tech consumerism are materializing—albeit in a less radical manner—in broader movements toward refurbished gadgets, and in a resurgence in retro electronic devices led by younger generations fatigued by today’s digital overload
But keeping up the lifestyle is a challenge

title: Using the Power of the Government to Win Elections
excerpt: T he principle that government ought to be administered for the benefit of all citizens, not on behalf of one political party, lies at the core of America’s dem
body: T he principle that government ought to be administered for the benefit of all citizens, not on behalf of one political party, lies at the core of America’s democratic enterprise

The Trump administration couldn’t care less: It appears to see the federal government not as something to steward on behalf of all Americans, but as an opportunity—a set of levers it can pull on to protect its reign
America’s adherence to this principle of executive neutrality has never been perfect, but as a norm it has been honored more than breached
When I served as a political appointee in the Department of Homeland Security under President George W
Bush, the idea that the secretaries of defense or homeland security or the attorney general would have ever appeared at a political rally was unimaginable
Their roles were too important to national security to risk being perceived as partisan operatives

Its members are willing to use the public power at their disposal to do what they can to give Republicans an edge in this fall’s elections—to campaign for candidates from their public pulpits, to push broadcast-news coverage in a more favorable direction, to try to strong-arm the U.S

Postal Service into regulating mail-in balloting into oblivion, to threaten withholding FEMA relief funds from those states that don’t elect Republican candidates, to release pro–Donald Trump propaganda funded by taxpayer dollars, and, the most crass offense, to offer $5,000 checks to voters if Republicans win
Some of these tactics are in a legal gray area; others are plainly forbidden
But all of them are violations of the precept that the party in power should not tilt the electoral scales toward itself
The most egregious area of activity has been the total disregard administration officials have shown for the Hatch Act
The law, passed in 1939, imposes limits on certain government employees to ensure that these officials in their executive functions are above partisan political activity

Federal employees may not use their official authority to influence an election, though they can engage in political activity when they are off the clock, and restricted employees (which includes all national-security and law-enforcement personnel) may not “take an active part” in any political campaign
The law is still being enforced, but only against everyday federal employees

For example, the DHS inspector general recently found that some FEMA disaster responders had violated the Hatch Act when they skipped providing assistance to homes with pro-Trump signs after Hurricane Milton
But in Trump world, the law is for thee and not for me
Attorney General Todd Blanche has turned out to be something of a serial campaigner
He traveled to Long Island to give a speech at a rally for Bruce Blakeman, a Republican running for governor of New York
He gave a speech at the Republican National Committee’s midterm convention

He stumped for Michael Whatley, a Senate candidate from North Carolina. [ Read: The problem with Trump’s new taxpayer-funded ads ] Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth went to the Iowa State Fair to support Republican Representative Zach Nunn
Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy gave an August speech at a super-PAC event supporting GOP candidates in Michigan in which he mixed official business with praise for a Republican candidate

And, as The Atlantic has reported , Trump even went so far as to have a secret points-system competition among his Cabinet members to see who could travel to the greatest number of competitive House districts over the summer (though, to be clear, not all of that travel was overtly in violation of the Hatch Act)
Who is supposed to do anything about any of this? That responsibility falls to the Office of Special Counsel , whose head Trump fired early in his second term
He then nominated as his replacement a host of a far-right podcast , whose past behavior and qualifications were so poor that even the Senate Republicans could not support him
Despite not having a permanent leader, the OSC has managed to launch a Hatch Act investigation of one person of great interest to the president: former Special Counsel Jack Smith
The investigation is in response to a complaint that Smith sought quick criminal-trial dates for Trump as a means of influencing the 2024 election
Perhaps less egregious but no less troubling has been the erosion of the traditional neutrality of the Federal Communications Commission

For years, the FCC’s equal-time rule (not to be confused with the broader, now-repealed fairness doctrine) was the legal embodiment of the principle of the government’s neutrality among the different political factions
The rule required that if a broadcaster allowed a candidate to appear, it “shall afford equal opportunities to all other such candidates” for that office
Exceptions were possible for bona fide news events

The rule has generally been interpreted quite leniently—allowing, for example, programs such as Access Hollywood , Today , and The Howard Stern Show to host political candidates on the air without requiring their opponents be allowed the same
Under Trump’s FCC chairman, Brendan Carr, the agency has perfected the use of its authority to threaten broadcasters it perceives as anti-Trump
In late January 2026, the FCC issued new “guidance” aimed at late-night-TV hosts , effectively reversing the long-standing leniency
Some networks responded by changing what they put on their shows
CBS pulled an interview of James Talarico , the Democrat from Texas running for Senate, from Stephen Colbert’s late-night show
Without a doubt, the single most noteworthy effort the FCC has undertaken involves its obsessive pursuit of ABC
The effort to influence the network’s programming began in late 2025 when Carr urged ABC (owned by Disney) to pull Jimmy Kimmel from the air after he inartfully commented on Charlie Kirk’s death
Appearing on a right-wing podcast , Carr said: “We can do this the easy way or the hard way
These companies can find ways to change conduct, to take action, frankly, on Kimmel, or there’s going to be additional work for the FCC ahead”—seemingly a not-so-veiled threat of licensure action
Though Kimmel was suspended, he eventually returned to the air

title: Connecting AI agents to enterprise knowledge
excerpt: For all the data that AI systems continually amass and analyze, enterprise AI agents often suffer from a curious shortcoming: a lack of knowledge
body: For all the data that AI systems continually amass and analyze, enterprise AI agents often suffer from a curious shortcoming: a lack of knowledge
More than data, knowledge is the understanding of what the data means in the context of individual organizations
AI agents need this understanding to reason about situations, make decisions, and ultimately take actions
Without sufficient knowledge, agents are prone to making flawed and unreliable decisions
A lack of knowledge, our research finds, is a major reason agentic AI use cases never make it to production
Competitive pressure is making it urgent to address this
Organizations need to deploy and scale more of their agentic projects to capture the efficiency gains AI promises
Falling short risks wasting the investment already sunk into these projects, and it cedes ground to rivals already putting their agents to work more effectively
DOWNLOAD THE REPORT The purpose of this report, which is based on a survey of 300 data, AI, and other technology executives, is threefold

First, it seeks to gauge organizations’ agentic knowledge capabilities (i.e., their ability to give AI agents a full contextual understanding of the data they ingest) across semantic knowledge, episodic memory, and procedural knowledge
Second, the report probes the challenges organizations face in improving access to knowledge and ultimately to getting more agent use cases into production
Third, it explores the measures organizations are taking to overcome these challenges
The key findings include the following: Data and knowledge weaknesses consistently stall AI agent progress
On average, only around a third (34%) of organizations’ agentic AI projects make it into production
Legacy data systems, security and privacy concerns, and a lack of knowledge and context are the key points of failure
Strong knowledge capabilities correlate with agent success

A small group of production leaders (organizations where on average 61% of agentic projects advance beyond pilot) have stronger knowledge capabilities than the rest, especially when it comes to semantics
This advantage tracks closely with their higher production rate
Fragmented data hugely complicates knowledge access
Data fragmentation (the inadequate sharing of data across systems) was most commonly cited as a top challenge to expanding agents’ access to knowledge (cited by 55%)
Production leaders, by contrast, are more likely to see security and privacy concerns as a major concern (cited by 72% of this group)
Most firms aim to strengthen the link between data and agents
Among steps that can yield higher quality agent decisions, executives expect the biggest impact to come from strengthening the structural foundation between the organization’s data and its AI agents
The experts we interviewed see a knowledge layer as a prime way to achieve this
Investment priorities to boost knowledge range from pipelines to knowledge graphs

To expand agent access to knowledge, organizations will prioritize investments in retrieval technologies, like ingestion pipelines, AI-ready APIs, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG); in AI evaluation agents; and in knowledge graphs

title: Bringing predictive analytics to the agentic AI era
excerpt: In 2026, the question for enterprise AI is no longer whether predictive models can outperform statistical forecasts—that argument is settled
body: In 2026, the question for enterprise AI is no longer whether predictive models can outperform statistical forecasts—that argument is settled
The big question now is how to enable predictive systems to act on their own conclusions without drifting from business intent

The frontier has moved from prediction to autonomous decision making, and the gap between leaders and laggards is widening accordingly. “Enterprises are done with a backward-looking point of view; they want to be more forward-thinking,” says Vishal Gupta, partner at research firm Everest Group
DOWNLOAD THE REPORT Intelligent analytics, powered by technologies like deep learning and generative AI, are making this possible
Real-time training allows AI to evolve continuously instead of waiting for quarterly refreshes
In addition, the data that newer predictive engines rely upon has expanded to encompass not just neat, numerical records but also messy, unstructured sources of insight-rich interactions
As a result, AI-powered analytics are moving enterprises from passive hindsight to pragmatic foresight

AI takes predictive analytics—a broad discipline that includes predictive modeling, data prep, analysis workflows, interpretation of results, and decision-making applications—to new heights. “In many ways I think the word ‘analytics’ is giving way to AI,” says Gupta. “Everything is becoming AI.” Download the report This content was produced by Insights, MIT Technology Review’s custom content arm, not its editorial staff

title: People really hate AI, so why can’t they get enough?
excerpt: People hate AI and can't stop using it: More US adults expect AI to hurt them than help them—yet ChatGPT just hit a billion monthly users
body: People hate AI and can't stop using it: More US adults expect AI to hurt them than help them—yet ChatGPT just hit a billion monthly users
The Venn diagram of AI skeptics and AI users is rapidly becoming a circle

It's not the tech, it's the push: The real frustration isn't artificial intelligence itself—it's the relentless corporate drive to inject it everywhere, while promising the biggest social upheaval in generations

This time might actually be different: Unlike social media's walled gardens, AI still offers genuine consumer choice and real regulatory momentum—all 50 US states have passed or proposed AI laws. " data-chronoton-post-id="1145682" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> Over the summer I talked to the CEO of Springboards, a startup building an LLM that’s designed to come up with a wider variety of responses than its mainstream rivals do
At the start of the call, he said something that’s been stuck in my head since: “We often say that we’re a self-loathing AI company
We don’t know if we really like what we’re doing.” “I guess that makes me a self-loathing AI journalist,” I replied
But I do not love many of the things the technology I write about has become: warped by hype , steered by zealots , inescapable
The CEO of Springboards and I are far from alone
Around the world, a love/hate attitude toward AI is very much the vibe right now
On the one hand, public feelings are souring fast
According to the Pew Research Center, more adults in the US think AI will have a negative impact on them personally, and on society in general, than expect a positive one
The pessimism is strongest among the young
More than half of people worldwide say that AI products and services make them nervous, according to a report from Stanford University
In a Gallup poll in May, 71% of US adults said they would oppose construction of a new AI data center in their area, far more than the 53% who said they would oppose a new nuclear power plant
And in an NBC poll in March, AI was less popular than ICE
Yet the number of people using AI is still skyrocketing
ChatGPT hit a billion monthly users in May, according to the market analysis firm Sensor Tower
Google DeepMind’s Gemini is close behind, logging 950 million users in July
According to Pew, half of US adults now say they use a chatbot , more than twice the number who said they did in 2023
One in four people say they do so every day
And it’s a global habit: More than a third of adults across all 38 OECD countries (a group of the world’s wealthiest democracies) report having used generative AI tools in the last three months
All these surveys paint a picture of two contradictory truths: A lot of people really do not like AI and a lot of people cannot get enough of it
What’s going on? It’s possible that these are two distinct groups, but I doubt it
The numbers don’t add up unless the Venn diagram is on its way to being a circle
It’s also possible that the more people use AI, the more negative their opinions about it will be
There’s at least a correlation to back this up : The Global North, where adoption is highest, skews pessimistic
In the Global South, where adoption levels are lower, people are more optimistic

But here’s what I really think is going on: When people say they hate AI it’s not the technology they dislike but, rather, the relentless drive of the companies behind it to push the tech upon us in as many ways as possible
They’re telling us to brace for the biggest social and economic upheaval in generations
How do they expect people to feel? In many ways, we’ve been here before
We saw a similar dynamic play out with social media over the last 20 years
Billions flocked to Facebook and Twitter despite mounting techlash against the companies that ran those services
With social media there wasn’t much anyone could do
Quitting a platform meant losing all your content and connections, giving you the choice to suck it up or start over
But with AI there’s still a chance for people to have some sway
There’s certainly more political appetite for regulation this time around

All 50 US states have either passed or proposed laws governing the development and deployment of AI , creating a patchwork of more than 2,100 bills across the country—a tenfold increase in three years

And with a number of top-class open-source alternatives to Google and OpenAI and Anthropic already on the market, there’s also (for now, at least) the potential for more consumer choice and the market pressure that goes with it.  I don’t want to be naïve
Trillion-dollar companies are hard to move
But what comes next is not as inevitable as those companies often imply

title: Optogenetics wins the Nobel – one neuroscience breakthrough in a line of technological innovations helping scientists map and control the brain
url:
<title>Optogenetics wins the Nobel – one neuroscience breakthrough in a line of technological innovations helping scientists map and control the brain</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763993/original/file-20261005-60-gxnx1q.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C2121%2C1414&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Optogenetics is illuminating the inner workings of the brain. </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/artificial-intelligence-brain-with-fiber-optic-royalty-free-image/2216010511">akinbostanci/iStock via Getty Images Plus</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The brain is unbelievably complicated, which is both daunting and fascinating for <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=z3XmbfYAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">neuroscientists like me</a>. In the space of a cubic millimeter – about the size of a single poppy seed – there are <a href="https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adk4858">tens of thousands of neurons and other brain support cells</a>, all influencing each other’s function.</p>

<p>How do neuroscientists make sense of this complexity? And how did they get to the point where they could simply <a href="https://theconversation.com/how-pond-algae-led-to-a-nobel-prize-and-a-new-way-to-study-the-brain-293579">shine different colors of light on the brain</a> to control neuron activity?</p>

<p>The answer is one step at a time, with a lot of help from technology. </p>

<p>Revisiting some of the technological advances that have supported researchers’ current understanding of how the brain works can point to where the field of neuroscience might be going next. There is a rough pattern to the technological advances that have led neuroscience to the present day: visualize the brain, measure its function and then control it.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763999/original/file-20261005-50-klkrbo.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Presentation screen at Nobel Prize announcement, showing a diagram of a mouse with an optical fiber attached to its head" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763999/original/file-20261005-50-klkrbo.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763999/original/file-20261005-50-klkrbo.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763999/original/file-20261005-50-klkrbo.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763999/original/file-20261005-50-klkrbo.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763999/original/file-20261005-50-klkrbo.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763999/original/file-20261005-50-klkrbo.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763999/original/file-20261005-50-klkrbo.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Optogenetics uses light to control neuronal activity.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/karolinska-institute-neuroscience-professor-abdel-el-manira-news-photo/2298088451">Jonathan Nackstrand/AFP via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Using light to influence neuronal function, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/ijnp/pyv079">known as optogenetics</a>, allows neuroscientists to manipulate what neurons do millisecond by millisecond. The researchers whose work led to this technique won the <a href="https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/2026/press-release/">2026 Nobel Prize in physiology or medicine</a>.</p>

<p>The level of control afforded by optogenetics suggests that the ability to therapeutically adjust brain activity in ways that previously sounded like fantasy could be on the horizon, including <a href="https://doi.org/10.3390/biom12020269">restoring eyesight</a>, <a href="https://www.med.unc.edu/pharm/bryan-roths-groundbreaking-research-on-dreadds-highlighted/">reducing pain and treating diseases</a> like epilepsy and mental health disorders.</p>

<h2>Visualizing the brain</h2>

<p>Dollops of color and magnification are how neuroscientists came to know what neurons look like and how they connect to each other. </p>

<p>In the late 1800s, Spanish neuroscientist and artist <a href="https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/1906/cajal/biographical/">Santiago Ramon y Cajal</a> painted what he saw through the microscope. He looked at samples of brain tissue <a href="https://embryo.asu.edu/pages/golgi-staining-technique-image">stained with silver</a> to make individual neurons visible, a technique developed by the Italian neuroscientist <a href="https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/1906/golgi/biographical/">Camillo Golgi</a>. </p>

<p>As he painted, Cajal wondered about how neurons might influence each other through their connections. The ideas he developed <a href="https://doi.org/10.5406/amerjpsyc.131.3.0369">form the foundation</a> of how the brain learns and remembers. The work of these scientists won them the <a href="https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/1906/summary/">1906 Nobel Prize in physiology or medicine</a>.</p>

<p>In the 1970s, researchers developed another version of applying color to the brain called <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0301-0082(00)00019-8">anterograde and retrograde tracing</a>. These methods let neuroscientists map different pathways between neurons in the brain.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/tIWSt3aNH24?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">The connectome of the brain is incredibly complex.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Today, the brain can be visualized in much finer detail using technologies such as <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41592-025-02988-6">electron microscopy</a>, which involves firing a stream of electrons at an object to develop an image at atomic resolution,  and <a href="https://news.mit.edu/2025/brief-history-expansion-microscopy-0423">expansion microscopy</a>, which uses the same type of gel inside baby diapers to physically enlarge a tissue sample to visualize each cell and its connections. These techniques, combined with artificial intelligence algorithms, are what allow scientists to see the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adk4858">complexity within a cubic millimeter of brain tissue</a>.</p>

<p>Magnetic resonance imaging has also profoundly influenced how researchers understand the brain. Functional MRI lets neuroscientists noninvasively eavesdrop on brain activity by measuring blood flow <a href="https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1204471">across the entire brain</a>. In 2003, the Nobel Prize in physiology or medicine was awarded to the <a href="https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/2003/summary/">development of MRI techniques</a> that make functional MRI possible: fast imaging sequences and spatial encoding.</p>

<p>All of these visualization and magnification methods <a href="https://hms.harvard.edu/news/new-field-neuroscience-aims-map-connections-brain">form the field of connectomics</a>: mapping all the connections between neurons.</p>

<h2>Measuring neuronal activity</h2>

<p>On top of visualizing the brain’s structures and layout, the ability to manipulate electricity has allowed researchers to learn how neurons communicate.</p>

<p>Neuroscientists <a href="https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/1963/hodgkin/biographical/">Alan Hodgkin</a> and <a href="https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/1963/huxley/facts/">Andrew Huxley</a> won the <a href="https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/1963/summary/">1963 Nobel Prize in physiology or medicine</a> for their work on capturing and measuring the electrical impulses that neurons create. Neurons propagate these <a href="https://doi.org/10.1113/jphysiol.2001.014118">action potentials</a> to communicate with each other.</p>

<p>Today, the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1126/science.abf4588">probes that neuroscientists use</a> to measure the electrical activity of neurons can listen in on the activity of hundreds of neurons from different brain areas at the same time.</p>

<p>Research using simultaneous recording methods is upending scientists’ understanding of how the brain works: A series of studies published in 2025 showed that while an animal is making a decision, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-09226-1">95% of the brain</a> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-09235-0">is actively involved</a> in that process, not just neurons in brain areas typically associated with decision-making.</p>

<h2>Controlling neurons</h2>

<p>The ability to control the activity of specific neurons has been around since the late 1980s when French neurosurgeon <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=eRdmFqYAAAAJ&amp;hl=fr">Alim-Louis Benabid</a> developed the technique of <a href="https://theconversation.com/brain-stimulation-can-rewire-and-heal-damaged-neural-connections-but-it-isnt-clear-how-research-suggests-personalization-may-be-key-to-more-effective-therapies-182491">deep brain stimulation</a> to help ameliorate the symptoms of Parkinson’s disease. </p>

<p>Deep brain stimulation acts like a pacemaker for brain activity. Today, researchers are studying the potential use of this technique to relieve symptoms of mental health disorders, including <a href="https://theconversation.com/treating-mental-illness-with-electricity-marries-old-ideas-with-modern-tech-and-understanding-of-the-brain-podcast-195071">obsessive compulsive disorder</a>, <a href="https://theconversation.com/depression-recovery-can-be-hard-to-measure-new-research-on-deep-brain-stimulation-shows-how-objective-biomarkers-could-help-make-treatment-more-precise-213647">major depression</a> and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41591-022-01941-w">binge eating</a>, to name a few.</p>

<p>While the results can be dramatic, deep brain stimulation is a relatively crude method for controlling neuronal activity because the implanted electrode influences all cells nearby. But researchers are developing more precise and higher resolution techniques to both study and adjust brain function.</p>

<p>One of the coolest things about optogenetic techniques is that they may also help treat disease. Researchers are currently testing whether optogenetics can alleviate symptoms or enhance the treatment of <a href="https://doi.org/10.3390/biom12020269">vision loss</a>, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s10571-024-01486-1">Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson disease</a> <a href="https://doi.org/10.4103/1673-5374.213532">epilepsy, multiple sclerosis</a>, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.copbio.2025.103262">diabetes, cancer</a> and more.</p>

<h2>Neuroscience goes viral</h2>

<p>Neurons don’t naturally respond to the lights used in optogenetics. So neuroscientists must instruct them to renovate their cell walls so that some of their proteins are responsive to light. Scientists do this by sending instructions directly to neurons via a harmless virus. </p>

<p>Optogenetics is not the only neuroscience technique that leverages viruses to deliver instructions to neurons. So does a method called <a href="https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0700293104">designer receptors exclusively activated by designer drugs, or DREADDs</a> for short.</p>

<p>Like optogenetics, DREADDs give neuroscientists the ability to control neuronal activity. While optogenetics uses light to zero in on a specific group of neurons to control their activity, DREADDs does this chemically – like a lock and key set that only works on certain types of neurons or a specific brain area. </p>

<p>DREADDs uses the same harmless virus to instruct neurons to alter their chemical receptors so that they respond only to specific drugs. <a href="https://cen.acs.org/biological-chemistry/biotechnology/human-trial-chemogenetic-brain-therapy/104/web/2026/08">Several clinical trials</a> are testing whether this technique could be used to treat conditions like Parkinson’s, epilepsy and neuropathic pain.</p>

<p>In the future, a surgical procedure involving red or blue light might restore vision or stop the progression of neurodegenerative diseases in their tracks. Or a cocktail of medicines might reduce anxiety or treat epilepsy. These treatments will be the culmination of decades of work developing methods to pinpoint where the brain is dysfunctional, and to refine or change the activity of neurons in those areas.</p>

<p>If you ask me, the future of neuroscience is looking bright.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/293619/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

body: Optogenetics is illuminating the inner workings of the brain. akinbostanci/iStock via Getty Images Plus The brain is unbelievably complicated, which is both daunting and fascinating for neuroscientists like me
In the space of a cubic millimeter – about the size of a single poppy seed – there are tens of thousands of neurons and other brain support cells , all influencing each other’s function

How do neuroscientists make sense of this complexity? And how did they get to the point where they could simply shine different colors of light on the brain to control neuron activity? The answer is one step at a time, with a lot of help from technology
Revisiting some of the technological advances that have supported researchers’ current understanding of how the brain works can point to where the field of neuroscience might be going next
There is a rough pattern to the technological advances that have led neuroscience to the present day: visualize the brain, measure its function and then control it
Optogenetics uses light to control neuronal activity
Jonathan Nackstrand/AFP via Getty Images Using light to influence neuronal function, known as optogenetics , allows neuroscientists to manipulate what neurons do millisecond by millisecond
The researchers whose work led to this technique won the 2026 Nobel Prize in physiology or medicine

The level of control afforded by optogenetics suggests that the ability to therapeutically adjust brain activity in ways that previously sounded like fantasy could be on the horizon, including restoring eyesight , reducing pain and treating diseases like epilepsy and mental health disorders
Visualizing the brain Dollops of color and magnification are how neuroscientists came to know what neurons look like and how they connect to each other
In the late 1800s, Spanish neuroscientist and artist Santiago Ramon y Cajal painted what he saw through the microscope
He looked at samples of brain tissue stained with silver to make individual neurons visible, a technique developed by the Italian neuroscientist Camillo Golgi
As he painted, Cajal wondered about how neurons might influence each other through their connections
The ideas he developed form the foundation of how the brain learns and remembers
The work of these scientists won them the 1906 Nobel Prize in physiology or medicine
In the 1970s, researchers developed another version of applying color to the brain called anterograde and retrograde tracing
These methods let neuroscientists map different pathways between neurons in the brain
The connectome of the brain is incredibly complex

Today, the brain can be visualized in much finer detail using technologies such as electron microscopy , which involves firing a stream of electrons at an object to develop an image at atomic resolution, and expansion microscopy , which uses the same type of gel inside baby diapers to physically enlarge a tissue sample to visualize each cell and its connections
These techniques, combined with artificial intelligence algorithms, are what allow scientists to see the complexity within a cubic millimeter of brain tissue
Magnetic resonance imaging has also profoundly influenced how researchers understand the brain
Functional MRI lets neuroscientists noninvasively eavesdrop on brain activity by measuring blood flow across the entire brain
In 2003, the Nobel Prize in physiology or medicine was awarded to the development of MRI techniques that make functional MRI possible: fast imaging sequences and spatial encoding
All of these visualization and magnification methods form the field of connectomics : mapping all the connections between neurons
Measuring neuronal activity On top of visualizing the brain’s structures and layout, the ability to manipulate electricity has allowed researchers to learn how neurons communicate
Neuroscientists Alan Hodgkin and Andrew Huxley won the 1963 Nobel Prize in physiology or medicine for their work on capturing and measuring the electrical impulses that neurons create
Neurons propagate these action potentials to communicate with each other
Today, the probes that neuroscientists use to measure the electrical activity of neurons can listen in on the activity of hundreds of neurons from different brain areas at the same time

Research using simultaneous recording methods is upending scientists’ understanding of how the brain works: A series of studies published in 2025 showed that while an animal is making a decision, 95% of the brain is actively involved in that process, not just neurons in brain areas typically associated with decision-making

Controlling neurons The ability to control the activity of specific neurons has been around since the late 1980s when French neurosurgeon Alim-Louis Benabid developed the technique of deep brain stimulation to help ameliorate the symptoms of Parkinson’s disease
Deep brain stimulation acts like a pacemaker for brain activity

Today, researchers are studying the potential use of this technique to relieve symptoms of mental health disorders, including obsessive compulsive disorder , major depression and binge eating , to name a few

<title>US migrant flights to Liberia evoke troubling history of sending people deemed unwanted to the West African nation</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763625/original/file-20261002-50-pscz07.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C3969%2C2646&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Liberian national police officers stand guard awaiting a plane carrying migrants deported from the United States to land in Harbel, Liberia, on Aug. 20, 2026. </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/liberias-national-police-officers-stand-guard-for-a-plane-news-photo/2290658064?phrase=liberia%20deportation&amp;adppopup=true">Matthew Jacobs / AFP via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/29/us/politics/supreme-court-deportations-third-country.html?searchResultPosition=1">Supreme Court’s recent decision</a> to temporarily allow the United States to resume deporting migrants to third-country destinations could see the resumption of flights to Liberia.</p>

<p>About the size of Ohio, the West African country is <a href="https://www.afp.com/en/us-has-deported-25000-third-countries-under-secretive-deals-report">one of 35 countries</a> the Trump administration is paying to shelter and feed Latin Americans and others living in the U.S. without proper legal status. Some of those receiving nations have a <a href="https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/9/29/us-supreme-court-allows-trump-to-continue-third-country-deportations">reputation for corruption and human rights abuses</a>, and in most cases, those being deported have no links to the host nation.</p>

<p>The policy may ultimately be deemed unconstitutional, but on Sept. 29, 2026, the Supreme Court justices gave the green light for flights to continue while they consider the policy’s legality.</p>

<p>So far, at least 20 U.S. deportees have been flown to Liberia. One Colombian national who arrived in the African nation on Aug. 20 <a href="https://www.cbsnews.com/news/liberia-first-group-third-country-deportees-from-u-s/">told PBS</a>: “Honestly, I had never heard of Liberia.” </p>

<p>While those being deported to Liberia may not be familiar with the country, the same can’t be said for American policymakers. Unlike <a href="https://www.thirdcountrydeportationwatch.org/">the other countries</a> participating in the Trump administration’s efforts, Liberia has a long history with American immigration policy.</p>

<p>As a <a href="https://journalism.richmond.edu/faculty/kmasters/">scholar who has written about that history</a>, I see echoes of past U.S. efforts to move nonwhite people to Liberia in the latest removals. Indeed, it is those past events that gave Liberia its name. </p>

<h2>Liberia’s American roots</h2>

<p>In the early 1800s, <a href="https://doi-org.newman.richmond.edu/10.1080/03086534.2025.2587140">Africa’s west coast</a> attracted American leaders who were looking for a place to send those they viewed as unwanted U.S. residents: free people of African descent. </p>

<p>The region became the endpoint for America’s first massive removal campaign, starting in 1820, focused on relocating Black people “<a href="https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/back-africa-movement/">back to Africa</a>.” The chief U.S. organization advocating for this effort was the <a href="https://www.whitehousehistory.org/the-american-colonization-society">American Colonization Society</a>, created in 1816. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763682/original/file-20261002-60-6xbatz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="An old map." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763682/original/file-20261002-60-6xbatz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763682/original/file-20261002-60-6xbatz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=385&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763682/original/file-20261002-60-6xbatz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=385&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763682/original/file-20261002-60-6xbatz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=385&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763682/original/file-20261002-60-6xbatz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=483&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763682/original/file-20261002-60-6xbatz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=483&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763682/original/file-20261002-60-6xbatz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=483&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">An American Colonization Society map of Liberia from 1835.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/american-colinization-map-of-liberia-illustration-by-g-f-news-photo/110605777?adppopup=true">Buyenlarge/Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>The initial wave of departures was made up of African American intellectuals, church leaders and merchants. The brutality and inhumanity that white Americans inflicted on free and enslaved Black people drove them out. Many abolitionists and Quakers – who <a href="https://www.pbs.org/thisfarbyfaith/journey_1/p_7.html">fought to ban slavery</a> – initially supported the colonization society’s removal efforts as a means for helping Black residents escape the cruelty of American laws, especially the <a href="https://www.history.com/articles/fugitive-slave-acts">Fugitive Slave Acts</a>. </p>

<p>But the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/hic3.12302">true driving force</a> was the slaveholder class, which held a majority in Congress. Those politicians demanded the deportations because they knew the presence of free Black people gave hope to the millions in bondage — who, in some states, outnumbered white people.</p>

<p>These early American settlers named their new home Liberia, for liberty. And by 1847, they fought the colonization society’s control over the land and turned the settlement into the <a href="https://www.liberianembassyus.org/article/liberia-celebrates-169-years-as-africas-oldest-independent-republic">first independent republic in Africa</a>. They set up towns and farms along the coastline, which had local indigenous communities estimated to be in the <a href="https://www.gilderlehrman.org/history-resources/essays/african-americans-and-making-liberia">hundreds of thousands</a>.</p>

<p>By the end of the century, some <a href="https://www.gilderlehrman.org/history-resources/essays/african-americans-and-making-liberia">16,000 Black Americans</a> made the journey, many against their will and all on the promise of a better life. Thousands more joined them, some from the Caribbean and at least 6,000 who were rescued from slave-trading vessels, intercepted and sent to Liberia by the U.S. Navy.</p>

<h2>A promised land</h2>

<p>The colonization society’s mass deportation plan was a nationwide effort with powerful political leaders and slaveholders like <a href="https://www.senate.gov/senators/FeaturedBios/Featured_Bio_Clay.htm">Henry Clay</a>, who was a U.S. senator, speaker of the House, secretary of state and three-time presidential candidate; <a href="https://www.britannica.com/biography/Francis-Scott-Key">Francis Scott Key</a>, a famous U.S. attorney best known for writing “The Star Spangled Banner”; and <a href="https://www.mountvernon.org/library/digitalhistory/digital-encyclopedia/article/bushrod-washington">Bushrod Washington</a>, a Supreme Court justice and nephew of George Washington.</p>

<p>Ten <a href="https://www.nps.gov/articles/000/to-forever-set-free-the-manumission-of-robert-green.htm">Southern state legislatures</a> endorsed the idea by passing laws that allowed the freeing of an enslaved person only when deportation out of the state was arranged and paid for. The colonization society raised the funds to pay for their removal to Liberia.</p>

<figure class="align-right zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763683/original/file-20261002-60-1d8ohy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A certificate of membership to the New York City Colonization Society" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763683/original/file-20261002-60-1d8ohy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=237&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763683/original/file-20261002-60-1d8ohy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=751&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763683/original/file-20261002-60-1d8ohy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=751&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763683/original/file-20261002-60-1d8ohy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=751&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763683/original/file-20261002-60-1d8ohy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=943&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763683/original/file-20261002-60-1d8ohy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=943&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763683/original/file-20261002-60-1d8ohy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=943&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">The New York City Colonization Society supported the migration of free Africans Americans to Africa.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/new-york-city-colonization-society-chapter-of-society-news-photo/529323673?adppopup=true">The New York Historical/Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Some abolitionists and future leaders, including <a href="https://quod.lib.umich.edu/j/jala/2629860.0014.204/--abraham-lincoln-and-the-politics-of-black-colonization?rgn=main;view=fulltext">Abraham Lincoln</a>, at first supported colonization because they believed it would help accelerate emancipation. But over time, and especially during the Civil War, most instead supported citizen rights for Black residents.</p>

<p>The effort was also opposed by powerful public intellectuals, including Frederick Douglass, who helped convince many — including Lincoln — of <a href="https://blackpast.org/global-african-history/1860-frederick-douglass-constitution-united-states-it-pro-slavery-or-anti-slavery/">the need to secure</a> freedom and justice for Black people in a country where they already lived.  </p>

<p>At least <a href="https://www.gilderlehrman.org/history-resources/essays/african-americans-and-making-liberia">20% of those who made the journey to Liberia</a> in the 1800s died of malaria. The rest dealt with supply shortages, severe weather, failed crops and hostility from indigenous communities. </p>

<p>But most white Americans <a href="https://www.loc.gov/exhibits/african/afam002.html">knew none of this</a>. They were told Liberia had fertile soil and a healthy climate; it was a promised land for Black people wishing to go home.</p>

<p>Harriet Beecher Stowe, in her best-selling novel “Uncle Tom’s Cabin,” furthered this notion by having her main characters, on a hair-raising and violent odyssey to escape enslavement, finally <a href="https://hillsdalecollegian.com/2013/10/the-irony-of-the-liberias-short-history/">find freedom and peace on a boat headed to Liberia</a>.</p>

<p>Douglass praised her novel in his newspaper, but for this last part of it, which <a href="https://daily.jstor.org/frederick-douglass-feud-over-uncle-toms-cabin/">he vehemently opposed</a>. Douglass <a href="https://frederickdouglasspapersproject.com/item/16716">wrote to Stowe</a>: “We are here, and here we are likely to remain. … We have grown up with this Republic; and I see nothing in our character … which compels the belief that we must leave the United States.”  </p>

<h2>A lingering US legacy</h2>

<p>The American Colonization Society’s strong influence on deportations ended with the Civil War, though the organization continued raising money and influencing U.S. policy until it was dissolved in 1964.</p>

<p>Other independent waves of migration to Liberia followed, especially as the end of Reconstruction unleashed white-led <a href="https://www.zinnedproject.org/collection/terror-to-overturn-reconstruction/">terrorism against Black communities</a> throughout the South. This included the Liberian Exodus Joint Stock Steamship Company, a Black-owned business that <a href="https://www.southcarolinapublicradio.org/podcast/south-carolina-from-a-to-z/2023-08-21/l-is-for-liberian-exodus">transported well-off African Americans</a> to Liberia in 1878. Its schooner carried some of Liberia’s soon-to-be-famous families from Charleston, South Carolina, to Liberia’s capital, Monrovia.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763686/original/file-20261002-50-6o0ul8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A crowd of people are seen next to a large ship." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763686/original/file-20261002-50-6o0ul8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763686/original/file-20261002-50-6o0ul8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=462&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763686/original/file-20261002-50-6o0ul8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=462&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763686/original/file-20261002-50-6o0ul8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=462&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763686/original/file-20261002-50-6o0ul8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=580&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763686/original/file-20261002-50-6o0ul8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=580&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763686/original/file-20261002-50-6o0ul8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=580&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">African Americans emigrants depart for Liberia on the steamship Laurada from Savannah, Ga., in 1896.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/african-americans-emigrants-depart-for-libera-africa-on-the-news-photo/640486501?adppopup=true">Illustrated American/Library of Congress/Corbis/VCG via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>In my view, what they accomplished along West Africa’s windward coast is astounding and, unfortunately, forgotten by most Americans. I’ve collected thousands of records from archives, including the U.S. National Archives, that show how surviving “Americo-Liberians,” as they called themselves, used grit and ingenuity to build large farming operations, grow merchant fleets, establish fisheries and spur other industries in their efforts to be integrated into Western global markets.</p>

<p>Yet for all the successes in difficult circumstances, Liberia in the 20th century remained in America’s shadow. After decades of fending off <a href="https://www.proquest.com/docview/1296744173?pq-origsite=gscholar&amp;fromopenview=true&amp;sourcetype=Scholarly%20Journals&amp;imgSeq=1">European attempts to absorb it into their colonial holdings</a>, Liberia sought refuge in its historical relationship with the U.S. And in the 1920s, the two countries began a “<a href="https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/documents/remarks-welcome-president-william-r-tolbert-jr-liberia">special friendship</a>.” At a time when <a href="https://jimcrowmuseum.ferris.edu/what.htm">Jim Crow laws</a> ravaged the American South, U.S. business interests created a plantation economy in Liberia rooted in resource extraction that enriched large U.S. companies, including <a href="https://doi.org/10.2307/jj.26193395">Firestone Tire</a> and <a href="https://ueaeprints.uea.ac.uk/id/eprint/85844/">Republic Steel</a>. </p>

<p>Archival records show the corruption that grew from deals benefiting the few at the expense of the many that became a long-term driver in the country’s political instability, resulting in civil strife and <a href="https://www.worldeconomics.com/Wealth/Liberia.aspx">poverty that has wracked</a> the country for decades.</p>

<h2>Coming full circle</h2>

<p>For many of the <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/21/us/politics/us-liberia-deportees-payment.html">1,200 people</a> earmarked for deportation to Liberia in the coming months by the U.S. government, landing in the capital, Monrovia, may feel cruel. That it was once a thriving city of Black elites whose forebearers arrived there from America may feel meaningless. </p>

<p>The circumstances of their deportations to Liberia are obviously very different form earlier waves. Those being deported today weren’t captured and sold into bondage; many left home to escape civil war, gang violence or starvation. </p>

<p>But there is a common driver between American policymakers now and those in the 19th century in encouraging and enforcing deportation to Liberia: a desire to rid the U.S. of nonwhite people deemed to represent a problem at home.</p>

<p>In December 2026, the Supreme Court will hear arguments and ultimately decide the constitutionality of this desire, as written into today’s rapid deportation policies.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/293186/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />
