body: Liberian national police officers stand guard awaiting a plane carrying migrants deported from the United States to land in Harbel, Liberia, on Aug. 20, 2026

Matthew Jacobs / AFP via Getty Images The Supreme Court’s recent decision to temporarily allow the United States to resume deporting migrants to third-country destinations could see the resumption of flights to Liberia

About the size of Ohio, the West African country is one of 35 countries the Trump administration is paying to shelter and feed Latin Americans and others living in the U.S. without proper legal status
Some of those receiving nations have a reputation for corruption and human rights abuses , and in most cases, those being deported have no links to the host nation
The policy may ultimately be deemed unconstitutional, but on Sept. 29, 2026, the Supreme Court justices gave the green light for flights to continue while they consider the policy’s legality
So far, at least 20 U.S. deportees have been flown to Liberia

One Colombian national who arrived in the African nation on Aug. 20 told PBS : “Honestly, I had never heard of Liberia.” While those being deported to Liberia may not be familiar with the country, the same can’t be said for American policymakers
Unlike the other countries participating in the Trump administration’s efforts, Liberia has a long history with American immigration policy
As a scholar who has written about that history , I see echoes of past U.S. efforts to move nonwhite people to Liberia in the latest removals
Indeed, it is those past events that gave Liberia its name

Liberia’s American roots In the early 1800s, Africa’s west coast attracted American leaders who were looking for a place to send those they viewed as unwanted U.S. residents: free people of African descent

The region became the endpoint for America’s first massive removal campaign, starting in 1820, focused on relocating Black people “ back to Africa .” The chief U.S. organization advocating for this effort was the American Colonization Society , created in 1816
An American Colonization Society map of Liberia from 1835
Buyenlarge/Getty Images The initial wave of departures was made up of African American intellectuals, church leaders and merchants
The brutality and inhumanity that white Americans inflicted on free and enslaved Black people drove them out

Many abolitionists and Quakers – who fought to ban slavery – initially supported the colonization society’s removal efforts as a means for helping Black residents escape the cruelty of American laws, especially the Fugitive Slave Acts
But the true driving force was the slaveholder class, which held a majority in Congress
Those politicians demanded the deportations because they knew the presence of free Black people gave hope to the millions in bondage — who, in some states, outnumbered white people
These early American settlers named their new home Liberia, for liberty
And by 1847, they fought the colonization society’s control over the land and turned the settlement into the first independent republic in Africa
They set up towns and farms along the coastline, which had local indigenous communities estimated to be in the hundreds of thousands
By the end of the century, some 16,000 Black Americans made the journey, many against their will and all on the promise of a better life
Thousands more joined them, some from the Caribbean and at least 6,000 who were rescued from slave-trading vessels, intercepted and sent to Liberia by the U.S

A promised land The colonization society’s mass deportation plan was a nationwide effort with powerful political leaders and slaveholders like Henry Clay , who was a U.S. senator, speaker of the House, secretary of state and three-time presidential candidate; Francis Scott Key , a famous U.S. attorney best known for writing “The Star Spangled Banner”; and Bushrod Washington , a Supreme Court justice and nephew of George Washington
Ten Southern state legislatures endorsed the idea by passing laws that allowed the freeing of an enslaved person only when deportation out of the state was arranged and paid for
The colonization society raised the funds to pay for their removal to Liberia
The New York City Colonization Society supported the migration of free Africans Americans to Africa
The New York Historical/Getty Images Some abolitionists and future leaders, including Abraham Lincoln , at first supported colonization because they believed it would help accelerate emancipation
But over time, and especially during the Civil War, most instead supported citizen rights for Black residents

The effort was also opposed by powerful public intellectuals, including Frederick Douglass, who helped convince many — including Lincoln — of the need to secure freedom and justice for Black people in a country where they already lived
At least 20% of those who made the journey to Liberia in the 1800s died of malaria
The rest dealt with supply shortages, severe weather, failed crops and hostility from indigenous communities
But most white Americans knew none of this
They were told Liberia had fertile soil and a healthy climate; it was a promised land for Black people wishing to go home

Harriet Beecher Stowe, in her best-selling novel “Uncle Tom’s Cabin,” furthered this notion by having her main characters, on a hair-raising and violent odyssey to escape enslavement, finally find freedom and peace on a boat headed to Liberia
Douglass praised her novel in his newspaper, but for this last part of it, which he vehemently opposed

Douglass wrote to Stowe : “We are here, and here we are likely to remain. … We have grown up with this Republic; and I see nothing in our character … which compels the belief that we must leave the United States.” A lingering US legacy The American Colonization Society’s strong influence on deportations ended with the Civil War, though the organization continued raising money and influencing U.S. policy until it was dissolved in 1964
Other independent waves of migration to Liberia followed, especially as the end of Reconstruction unleashed white-led terrorism against Black communities throughout the South
This included the Liberian Exodus Joint Stock Steamship Company, a Black-owned business that transported well-off African Americans to Liberia in 1878
Its schooner carried some of Liberia’s soon-to-be-famous families from Charleston, South Carolina, to Liberia’s capital, Monrovia

title: Fewer Americans are getting help buying groceries from SNAP benefits as states grapple with the program’s cascade of changes

<title>Fewer Americans are getting help buying groceries from SNAP benefits as states grapple with the program’s cascade of changes</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763695/original/file-20261002-80-c36u64.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C7820%2C5213&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">As of Oct. 1, 2026, states must pay more to run SNAP.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Producer%20Prices/1946a6c64ea24a74a70b177634f7b945/photo">AP Photo/Allison Dinner</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The number of people enrolled in the Supplemental Nutritional Assistance Program is falling fast. The program formerly known as food stamps <a href="https://fna-bwbufwdzbabpezgc.z01.azurefd.us/sites/default/files/resource-files/snap-4fymonthly-9.pdf">helped roughly 42 million Americans</a> put food on the table in 2025.</p>

<p>As of June 2026, the most recent data available, the number of people enrolled in the program in the whole country had declined by <a href="https://fna-bwbufwdzbabpezgc.z01.azurefd.us/sites/default/files/resource-files/snap-persons-9.pdf">almost 13% to 36.4 million</a>. Among those no longer getting benefits are an <a href="https://www.cbpp.org/blog/with-school-year-starting-childrens-participation-in-snap-continues-rapid-decline">estimated 1.5 million children</a>.</p>

<p>What explains this decline?</p>

<p><a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/donald-trump/trump-food-stamps-economy-rcna245083">President Donald Trump</a> says a strong economy has driven down demand for the program.</p>

<p>It’s possible that some people have left the program because their incomes rose. But the enrollment decline has a lot to do with the big tax-and-spending package <a href="https://theconversation.com/big-legislative-package-shifts-more-of-snaps-costs-to-states-saving-federal-dollars-but-causing-fewer-americans-to-get-help-paying-for-food-260166">the president signed into law in July 2025</a>. </p>



<h2>States are struggling to keep up</h2>

<p>For example, the law caused some <a href="https://www.nilc.org/articles/what-new-federal-snap-restrictions-and-guidance-mean-for-immigrant-communities/">immigrants residing legally</a> in the country, such as refugees and those seeking asylum, to no longer be eligible for SNAP benefits.</p>

<p>In addition, <a href="https://apnews.com/article/snap-benefits-children-work-requirement-34f582040d8f35a6f44443cdc57692e4">more people enrolled in SNAP now may only get up to</a> three months of benefits if they don’t <a href="https://www.fna.usda.gov/snap/work-requirements">work, engage in training programs or volunteer</a> at least 80 hours a month. These work requirements previously applied only to adults up to the age of 54; that cutoff is rising to 64. Another change is that parents of older children ages 14-17 are now expected to meet these <a href="https://www.propel.app/snap/snap-work-requirements-full-guide/">work requirements</a>.</p>

<p>All states are phasing in these restrictions, but <a href="https://stateline.org/2026/09/23/more-americans-lose-snap-as-congress-weighs-food-stamps-future/">the number of people getting SNAP benefits</a> is falling much faster in some states than others. That includes <a href="https://www.arizonaagenda.com/p/the-truth-behind-arizona-s-snap-free-fall">Arizona, where enrollment has fallen by almost half</a>, along with <a href="https://stateline.org/2026/09/23/more-americans-lose-snap-as-congress-weighs-food-stamps-future/">Louisiana and Illinois</a>, where it’s down by about one-fifth. </p>

<p>And now, <a href="https://www.npr.org/2026/10/01/nx-s1-5985222/snap-benefits-program-october-change-funding">states must pay more to run SNAP</a>, which is federally funded but state-administered. </p>

<p>In <a href="https://polisci.richmond.edu/faculty/troof/">my research</a> on the history of SNAP, I’ve found that changes in the way states run their programs have a big impact on who can get help. States are struggling to adapt to new federal policies. As additional changes roll out, more families may lose access to SNAP.</p>

<p><iframe id="Bi09K" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/Bi09K/1/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="Line graph showing the growth and reduction in the number of Americans getting SNAP benefits over time."></iframe></p>

<h2>Covering more of the administrative costs</h2>

<p>As of Oct. 1, 2026, states have to pay 75% of all administrative costs, which include paying staff who manage the enrollment process and maintaining the program’s computer systems. Previously, states paid 50% of those costs. The federal government estimates that states and local governments will pay roughly <a href="https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/06/24/2026-12696/supplemental-nutrition-assistance-program-changes-in-federal-state-administrative-cost-sharing">US$17 billion more in administrative costs</a> over the next five years.</p>

<p>In the 2027 fiscal year, which began on Oct. 1, California – with the largest population of any state – will be responsible for paying roughly <a href="https://frac.org/blog/why-the-snap-administrative-cost-shift-threatens-state-budgets-and-program-operations">$670 million</a> more to run the program. Wyoming, with the smallest number of residents, will pay about <a href="https://frac.org/blog/why-the-snap-administrative-cost-shift-threatens-state-budgets-and-program-operations">$3 million more</a>.</p>

<p>Costs will be shifted to local governments in <a href="https://www.naco.org/resource/hr-1-and-supplemental-nutrition-assistance-program-snap-what-counties-should-know">nine of the 10 states</a> where SNAP is administered by counties.</p>

<h2>Looming changes tied to ‘payment error rates’</h2>

<p>State agencies and <a href="https://www.kctv5.com/2026/08/15/kansas-snap-enrollment-drops-sharply-new-requirements-take-hold/">some state legislatures</a> are imposing stricter rules and requiring applicants to provide more paperwork documenting their income, expenses and the number of people in their household.</p>

<p>Caseworkers in states such as Arizona have reportedly been overwhelmed with the paperwork. <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/20/us/politics/snap-food-stamps-arizona.html">Those seeking help</a> have spent hours trying to get through on phone lines and have faced monthslong delays.</p>

<p>States are taking these steps to get ready for another change that will roll out in October 2027. At that point, many states will also have to cover up to 15% of the costs of benefits for the first time since the program began in the 1960s.</p>

<p><a href="https://frac.org/wp-content/uploads/SNAP-Cost-Shift-Table.pdf">This cost</a> is much larger than the administrative costs and could be <a href="https://aldailynews.com/alabama-officials-warn-snap-changes-could-force-stark-choice-pay-more-cut-error-rate-or-end-program/">staggering for many states</a>. </p>

<p>How much a state pays will be based on its “payment error rate.” These error rates measure how much in benefits are paid above or below what families are actually entitled to based on their household size, income and expenses. It is <a href="https://www.fna.usda.gov/snap/qc">calculated based on an in-depth review</a> of a small sample of a state’s benefits payments each year.</p>

<p>These inaccurate payments are generally a result of <a href="https://www.fna.usda.gov/snap/qc">mistakes on the part of the applicant or their caseworker</a> – they rarely are the result of fraud. The payment error rate includes benefits paid to ineligible participants. It does not include payments never made to applicants who were eligible for benefits but wrongly denied them or incorrectly dropped from the program.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.cbpp.org/research/food-assistance/snap-tracker-people-are-losing-food-assistance-as-the-harmful-2025">Supporters of SNAP</a> argue that this makes states err on the side of denying benefits.</p>

<p><iframe id="yB8hm" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/yB8hm/2/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="Chart indicating the maximum benefits available through SNAP, according to the number of people in a household."></iframe></p>

<h2>Range of rates</h2>

<p>States with an error rate less than 6% won’t face new costs for benefits. But only nine <a href="https://fna-bwbufwdzbabpezgc.z01.azurefd.us/sites/default/files/resource-files/snap-qcfy25-per.pdf">states had rates that low</a> in 2025.</p>

<p>States with an error rate between 6% and 8% will be responsible for 5% of the costs of their residents’ SNAP benefits. States with an error rate between 8% and 10% will have to cover 10%. States with error rates over 10% will have to cover 15%. </p>

<p>There’s a weird twist: If a state has an <a href="https://www.medicaldaily.com/snap-error-rates-october-2027-penalty-states-usda-one-big-beautiful-bill-2026-476091">error rate over 13.32%</a>, it won’t have to pay part of the cost of residents’ SNAP benefits for up to two years as they would have had it been in the 6% to 13.32% range.</p>

<h2>Farm bill politics could play a role</h2>

<p>To reduce their error rates, <a href="https://aphsa.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/2026-06_APHSA-State-SNAP-Survey-Results.pdf">states need to invest</a> in more staff, training, technology and better application and verification procedures. But states had little time to do all that. The states’ share of costs slated to kick in as of October 2027 is based on the error rates in the fiscal year that ended in September 2026.</p>

<p>Organizations representing <a href="https://www.nga.org/advocacy-communications/letters-nga/nga-joins-coalition-letter-outlining-snap-recommendations/">state and local governments and social workers</a> are pushing for an across-the board two-year delay. </p>

<p>What’s more, legislation known as the “<a href="https://theconversation.com/topics/farm-bill-137627">farm bill</a>,” which sets policies for agriculture, conservation and food-related assistance like SNAP, is now ensnared in the dispute. <a href="https://www.agdaily.com/insights/farm-bill-hit-dead-end-issues-seem-insurmountable/">Democrats, whose support is needed</a> to pass the legislation in the Senate, would like to see most of the new SNAP changes repealed.</p>

<p>Congress aims to pass a farm bill roughly every five years, but the most recent one, which was finalized in 2018, <a href="https://www.wrtv.com/news/agriculture/farm-bill-set-expire/">has expired</a>.</p>

<p>Short of rolling back all the SNAP policy changes, many <a href="https://rollcall.com/2026/08/06/farm-bill-rejected-in-partisan-split-over-food-stamp-cost-sharing/">Democrats have refused to vote</a> for the farm bill unless it includes a two-year delay for all states in shouldering part of the cost of SNAP benefits. </p>

<p>If the Democratic Party holds a majority in one or both chambers of Congress after the 2026 midterm elections, their leverage could increase in these negotiations.</p>

<p>The Republican Party’s <a href="https://www.agriculture.senate.gov/agricultural-act-of-2026-farm-bill-20">version of the farm bill</a> now pending in the Senate includes a one-year delay in the benefits-funding changes. But it would increase the states’ burden even more than the policy planned for October 2027. That’s a nonstarter for Democrats.</p>

<h2>What states can do about all this</h2>

<p>Meanwhile, there are many signs that a large share of the people who have lost their SNAP benefits are <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/20/us/politics/snap-food-stamps-arizona.html">struggling to feed</a> their families. More people, for example, are <a href="https://www.arizonaagenda.com/p/the-truth-behind-arizona-s-snap-free-fall">seeking help from food pantries and banks</a>, which fear they will not be able to keep up with growing demand.</p>

<p>It’s hard to predict what might happen next.</p>

<p><a href="https://news.bloomberglaw.com/health-law-and-business/trumps-latest-food-stamp-cut-hits-states-wary-of-lasting-costs">SNAP’s higher costs</a> could force states and counties to raise taxes, cut spending on other programs or find ways to reduce spending on SNAP.</p>

<p>Officials in some states are saying that they <a href="https://www.hickenlooper.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/2025.06.24-Multi-Gov-Letter-on-SNAP_FINAL.pdf">may find they need</a> to <a href="https://www.cbsnews.com/news/snap-benefits-millions-lost-obbba-work-requirements/">drop the program altogether</a>.</p>

<p>Because states lack the authority to change benefit amounts or do much to directly limit who qualifies for the program, I believe more states will be tempted to add red tape to lower their error rates, reduce the number of people getting benefits, or both.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/292829/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

title: Why it’s more important than ever to jump-start entrepreneurial careers from the college classroom

<title>Why it’s more important than ever to jump-start entrepreneurial careers from the college classroom</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763435/original/file-20261001-60-o1rgw7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C3200%2C2133&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">By teaching entrepreneurship, colleges can better prepare students for a fast-changing job market and technological disruption.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/in-this-photo-illustration-a-georgia-institute-of-news-photo/1247576996?phrase=georgia%20tech%20business&amp;adppopup=true">Igor Golovniov/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Recent college graduates are facing a job market that’s only getting tougher. Their <a href="https://www.newyorkfed.org/research/college-labor-market#--:explore:unemployment">unemployment rate hit 5.7%</a>, compared to 4.1% for all workers, in June 2026. That may not sound like much, but it’s <a href="https://www.wsj.com/lifestyle/careers/americans-without-college-degrees-are-having-one-of-the-best-job-markets-in-years-5f37d00e">one of the worst</a> rates in the past 20 years. </p>

<p>Meanwhile, <a href="https://www.forbes.com/sites/michaeltnietzel/2026/02/23/unemployment-and-underemployment-rates-among-recent-college-graduates/">roughly 4 in 10</a> graduates are underemployed, which means they work in jobs that typically don’t require a college degree. That’s the highest rate since the COVID-19 pandemic. </p>

<p>As an <a href="https://ece.gatech.edu/directory/raghupathy-sivakumar">educator</a> for more than 25 years, I see the growing anxiety every day. In a change from years past, parents are now peppering me with questions: How can their kids leverage their college education in such a fast-changing world? Will they learn skills in school that will soon be antiquated once they graduate? </p>

<p>What’s essential to understand is that technology adoption cycles have accelerated at a breathtaking rate over the past few years. While the telephone and television took decades to reach 100 million users, ChatGPT and TikTok <a href="https://www.reuters.com/technology/chatgpt-sets-record-fastest-growing-user-base-analyst-note-2023-02-01/">attained that threshold</a> in a matter of months. Colleges need to adapt their curricula accordingly. </p>

<p>Georgia Tech, where I teach engineering, has focused on pushing entrepreneurship across our campus since 2014. We’re seeing encouraging signs from our follow-ups with graduating students that it’s helping their early careers.</p>

<p>I believe one of the best ways to adjust to these changes is to embed entrepreneurial experiences throughout college. Such hands-on learning, in turn, develops versatile, adaptable talent, producing graduates who can pivot across jobs as industries, technologies and opportunities evolve. And this needn’t be confined to business students – young people in all majors can benefit. </p>

<h2>3 core lessons</h2>

<p>The educational value of entrepreneurship isn’t principally that every student will be able to start a company. It’s that entrepreneurial experiences <a href="https://create-x.gatech.edu/about-us">develop the capabilities</a> students need in a rapidly changing economy – and ultimately build more resilient careers. </p>

<p>Here are some ways educators can future-proof the college experience, based on what I’ve learned and applied at Georgia Tech.  </p>

<p><strong>Making adaptability a core skill:</strong> Students need to learn <a href="https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/223125">how to be nimble</a>. This means recognizing important changes in the landscape, identifying new problems and the opportunities they create, articulating a response and mobilizing the necessary resources. Ultimately, this approach will help students be prepared for the real world.</p>

<p>To impart these lessons, I believe colleges should provide hands-on opportunities to help students learn through experience before they enter the workforce. For example, they could encourage students to develop a business venture idea that addresses a newly created opportunity in the marketplace through accelerators, or short-term “boot camps” for young companies to help them grown quickly. One example is Greptile, a startup that came out of the <a href="https://www.greptile.com/">Georgia Tech CREATE-X accelerator</a>. </p>

<p>The goal isn’t that a startup will be launched – that depends on several factors coming together – but that the student gains the experience to understand a changing landscape. </p>

<p><strong>Understanding customer value:</strong> Colleges can also teach students how to think about customer value – namely, why the solution they’re working on matters to the consumers buying it. This isn’t just for business students. All students can gain from learning to think about the customers or clients they will deal with in their careers. In fact, students from 38 majors have participated in the <a href="https://create-x.gatech.edu/about-us">entrepreneurship programs at Georgia Tech</a>.</p>

<p>Through on-the-ground experience that requires them to find customers, students can learn about the real-world impact of the products and services they create. When students spend hundreds of hours selling their young startup to the outside world, they learn to understand value at a deep level.</p>

<p><strong>Emphasizing fundamentals:</strong> Fundamental skills are key because they outlast the technology underpinning the business. In fact, the more quickly specific technologies change, the more important a strong grounding in fundamentals becomes. This means it’s a smarter investment to offer, say, a fundamental course on wireless networking or deep learning concepts over a course that teaches specific wireless technologies or emphasizes the use of a specific model. A strong foundation gives students the tools to adapt to technologies that may not yet exist when they graduate. </p>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>The many paths toward entrepreneurship</h2>

<p>Another great advantage of entrepreneurial experiences is that they force students to deal with uncertainty, recognize opportunities, work around resource constraints and learn how to create value. </p>

<p>But other strategies work as well. A few examples are project-based learning, internships and interdisciplinary capstone classes that let students pursue independent research projects as their final course. </p>

<p>That said, entrepreneurial experiences provide an unusually concentrated and effective environment that requires students to solve problems, engage with customers and mobilize resources they don’t directly control – all while getting real-world feedback. </p>

<p>More and more universities and colleges understand this point and have ramped up support for entrepreneurial activity for their students, <a href="https://eship.cornell.edu/">such as Cornell</a> and the <a href="https://www.washington.edu/innovation/programs/">University of Washington</a>. At Georgia Tech, we have a <a href="https://www.wipo.int/documents/d/global-innovation-index/docs-en-2026-gii-2026-contributors-disrupting-the-disruptors.pdf">playbook that we have developed</a> through our experiences that follows the following principles: </p>

<p><strong>Embed entrepreneurship into the curriculum:</strong> One simple way for colleges to incorporate entrepreneurial experiences into their coursework is to offer an entrepreneurship minor to all students, regardless of major. This would offer the opportunity to a broader range of students who otherwise might miss out.</p>

<p><strong>Build a pathway to business creation:</strong> Entrepreneurial education is most effective when it leads to something bigger. To that end, many colleges are now offering a startup accelerator, <a href="https://entrepreneurship.mit.edu/accelerator/program/">including MIT</a>, <a href="https://entrepreneurship.rice.edu/rice-startup-accelerator">Rice University</a> and the <a href="https://undergraduates.utexas.edu/launchpad/seal">University of Texas</a>. </p>

<p>But more is needed: A startup pathway that caters to students at all stages can substantially broaden participation and impact, regardless of whether a business results. At Georgia Tech, we have a <a href="https://commercialization.gatech.edu/">learn/make/launch/scale pathway</a> that offers programs and resources for learning about entrepreneurship, building solutions, launching new ventures and eventually scaling them.</p>

<p><strong>Offer real venture experience:</strong> A successful model combines theoretical learning with hands-on experience. The confidence that students gain through that experience may be at least as important an educational outcome as the viability of the startups they launch. After all, since most startups <a href="https://hbr.org/2021/05/why-start-ups-fail">tend to fail</a>, confidence is a value that successful entrepreneurs have to sustain.  </p>

<h2>Transferring skills to the workforce</h2>

<p>There’s another important element that’s needed: private sector partnerships. Fortunately, entrepreneurial education is well aligned with the interests of universities’ traditional corporate partners.</p>

<p>These companies, especially those with established, successful business models, <a href="https://www.researchgate.net/publication/399057037">are eager</a> to hire students with a strong understanding of fundamentals and entrepreneurial confidence. This next generation can help the companies navigate the future. </p>

<p>Companies can also offer industry know-how, mentorship opportunities and financial and in-kind support. And they understand that students building a startup have to think <a href="https://www.researchgate.net/publication/386104454_Startups_can_offer_student_interns_real-life_advantages">beyond their own discipline</a> to succeed. For example, an engineering student will need to understand customers, pricing, finance, sales, operations, intellectual property and team building. That broader perspective can make them more effective when they enter a corporate environment full time. </p>

<p>The same capabilities can also translate into venture creation itself: The value of entrepreneurial education can be seen across both traditional workforce pathways and startup outcomes. Our experience at Georgia Tech offers evidence of both.</p>

<p>Startups launched by Georgia Tech students over the past decade have crossed <a href="https://create-x.gatech.edu/">US$4.5 billion</a> in aggregate total valuation and have created thousands of jobs. We’ve also found encouraging early evidence that students who gain confidence through these experiences have <a href="https://www.researchgate.net/publication/404299375_Entrepreneurship_Education_Shapes_Career_Trajectories_beyond_Entrepreneurial_Intentions">stronger career outcomes</a>. </p>

<p>Georgia Tech isn’t alone. The University System of Georgia has recently created a new role: a <a href="https://costasspirou.com/">chief innovation and entrepreneurial strategies officer</a> to lead an initiative across all of the state’s public colleges and universities. </p>

<p>Other universities are pursuing similar paths, including the <a href="https://www.cavalierdaily.com/article/2025/11/paul-cherukuri-leads-uvas-entrepreneurship-strategy-as-its-first-chief-innovation-officer">University of Virginia</a>, <a href="https://profiles.rice.edu/staff/adrian-tromel">Rice University</a> and <a href="https://news.cornell.edu/stories/2026/06/matt-marx-named-vice-provost-entrepreneurship-innovation-and-external-engagement">Cornell University</a>. All now have an institutionwide leadership position focused on entrepreneurship.</p>

<p>Taken together, these developments suggest that educators increasingly view entrepreneurship as more than just support for students who want to start companies. These steps will help ensure that when students walk across the stage to receive their diplomas, they can meet the challenges ahead of them.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/292831/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>What 1,000 years of golden roses tell us about popes’ authority and influence, from Leo IX to Leo XIV</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763505/original/file-20261001-50-s4jyso.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C5184%2C3456&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Pope John XXII presented the oldest surviving golden rose to a 14th-century count. The rose is now in the Musée de Cluny, a museum of medieval art in Paris.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cluny_Rosa_de_oro_04.JPG">Miguel Hermoso Cuesta/Wikimedia Commons</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/">CC BY-SA</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Almost every ceremonial object or ornament of the medieval papal monarchy has disappeared or lost its original purpose. Yet one survives: the golden rose.</p>

<p>On Sept. 26, 2026, during Pope Leo XIV’s visit to France, he traveled to Lourdes, home to <a href="https://theconversation.com/how-lourdes-became-a-byword-for-hope-174574">one of the world’s most famous shrines</a> to the Virgin Mary. After praying, Leo <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=B3y3R5vOuWg">presented a golden rose</a> to Our Lady of Lourdes – the fifth time he has <a href="https://aleteia.org/2025/10/13/pope-leo-presents-golden-rose-to-our-lady-of-fatima/">dedicated a rose</a> to a Marian shrine or image.</p>

<p>The ornate rose Leo offered to Lourdes is not that different from its medieval iterations. The <a href="https://www.musee-moyenage.fr/en/collection/golden-rose.html">oldest surviving rose</a> is now at the Musée de Cluny in Paris and dates from the early 1300s. Both are golden, with several <a href="https://www.liturgicalartsjournal.com/2023/03/the-tradition-of-rosa-doro-golden-rose.html">branches and buds</a>.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/4E5lVZxQQN4?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">Pope Leo XIV offered a golden rose in Lourdes as part of a four-day trip to France.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Yet who receives the roses, and why, has changed dramatically.</p>

<p>As a <a href="https://web.uri.edu/history/meet/joelle-rollo-koster-2/">medieval historian</a> researching the papacy, I frequently find mentions of the roses. They are ubiquitous in medieval chronicles – most of all, in papal <a href="https://www.burlington.org.uk/archive/back-issues/202608">accounting registers</a>. The <a href="https://www.burlington.org.uk/archive/back-issues/202608">history of the roses’ beneficiaries</a> reflects the history of the papacy and how its influence has shifted over the centuries.</p>

<h2>Roots of tradition</h2>

<p>Most medieval roses were made of gold and silver, adorned with precious stones such as sapphires and rubies. One of the buds formed a small receptacle that <a href="https://storicamente.org/indice-2026/rollo-koster_musk_papal_court_middle_ages">held some musk and balsam</a>, rare and expensive fragrances.</p>

<p>The Vatican Apostolic Archives have preserved the accounting registers that itemized many of the roses’ costs. On average, they weighed 11-16 ounces of precious metal and cost the equivalent of <a href="https://www.burlington.org.uk/archive/back-issues/202608">10 years of a laborer’s annual wage</a>. </p>

<p>The golden rose first appeared during the papacy of Leo IX. On April 18, 1049, the pope <a href="https://www.saintecroixenplaine.fr/decouvrir/historique/sainte-croix-en-plaine-a-travers-les-siecles">exempted a nunnery in Alsace</a> – now in Sainte-Croix-en-Plaine, France – from the legal authority and supervision of the local bishop. In return, the head of the nunnery was required to offer the pope a golden rose of some 2 ounces, or of equivalent value. At the time, roses were often used to <a href="https://daily.jstor.org/the-landlord-asks-for-a-christmas-rose/">symbolize a feudal pledge</a>: the submission of a vassal to a lord. </p>

<p>Within a couple of generations, the gift had changed direction: The pope now granted a rose. The first clearly documented case took place in 1096, when Urban II, touring France and preaching the First Crusade, granted it to <a href="https://www.burlington.org.uk/archive/back-issues/202608">Fulk of Anjou</a> to reward him for his <a href="https://independentcrusadersproject.ace.fordham.edu/items/show/150">willingness to participate</a>.</p>

<figure class="align-right zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763514/original/file-20261001-50-ty97w3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A scene of a man in green and orange robes kneeling in front of a man with red robes and a tall white hat." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763514/original/file-20261001-50-ty97w3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=237&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763514/original/file-20261001-50-ty97w3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=869&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763514/original/file-20261001-50-ty97w3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=869&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763514/original/file-20261001-50-ty97w3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=869&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763514/original/file-20261001-50-ty97w3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1092&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763514/original/file-20261001-50-ty97w3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1092&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763514/original/file-20261001-50-ty97w3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1092&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">A 13th-century illustration of a pope bestowing a golden rose on Laetare Sunday.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Remise_de_la_rose_d%E2%80%99or_par_un_pape_-_Presentation_of_the_golden_rose_by_a_pope.jpg">Musée de Cluny via Wikimedia Commons</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>From the 11th century on, the pope offered a rose once a year, on <a href="https://aleteia.org/2018/03/11/heres-why-popes-give-out-a-golden-rose/">Laetare Sunday</a>: the fourth Sunday of Lent, <a href="https://theconversation.com/what-are-the-origins-of-lent-155622">the period before Easter</a> when many Catholics commit to some form of penance. According to ceremonial books <a href="https://caeremonialeromanum.com/en/ordines-romani-andrieu/">called “ordines</a>,” the pope held the rose during the worship service, preached about its symbolism, and presented it to a recipient.</p>

<p>On that Sunday, gifting the rose reminded believers that while Lent was difficult, beauty and joy would emerge from it. The day was also a feast in honor of the recipient – typically <a href="https://www.oxfordreference.com/display/10.1093/acref/9780199545568.001.0001/acref-9780199545568-e-5299?p=emailASV6SP.8uLMHk&amp;d=/10.1093/acref/9780199545568.001.0001/acref-9780199545568-e-5299">the prefect of Rome</a>, who supervised the city’s jurisdictions and police.</p>

<h2>Diplomatic tool</h2>

<p>Eventually, the decision about who should receive the honor rested solely with the pope. Still, it was always bestowed upon those who wielded power: the prefect of Rome, emperors, kings, military leaders and defenders of Christian lands. Receiving the rose was a public acknowledgment that the recipient – usually a warrior – stood beside the pope in protecting the church.</p>

<p>In 1148, for example, Pope Eugene III <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IO8Oa63rudM">offered it to the king of Leon and Castile</a>, Alfonso VII. A century later, Pope Innocent IV gave it to <a href="https://www.britannica.com/biography/Ramon-Berenguer-IV">Raymond Berenger</a>, count of Provence. In both cases the pope rewarded the fight against Muslims, whom the Vatican saw as “infidels” or heretics.</p>

<p>The <a href="https://www.bloomsbury.com/us/avignon-and-its-papacy-13091417-9781442215344/">Avignon papacy</a> of the 14th century, a period when several popes resided in what is now southern France, accelerated this evolution. Away from Rome, and in the absence of a Roman prefect, the rose’s role as a negotiating tool intensified.</p>

<p>By the 14th century, <a href="https://storicamente.org/yh/rollo-koster_musk_papal_court_middle_ages">the ceremony had grown even more elaborate</a>. According to ceremonial books, the pope carried the rose in procession, while its beneficiary held the reins of his horse and kissed the pope’s feet – a gesture of submission. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">

            </figcaption>

<h2>Warriors, women – and shrines</h2>

<p>Historians can estimate how many people received the rose based on evidence available in the Vatican’s accounting registers and <a href="https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/gaetano-moroni">other historical records</a>. Over the years, more and more began to be presented to women, and then to shrines. This change shows the history of the papacy – and of its communication strategy. Simply put, the evolution of the rose followed the evolution of papal power itself. </p>

<p>The first few centuries of the rose were a period of conquests and Catholic expansionism, when conversion often came through war. With <a href="https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/great-western-schism-13781417/D0CBC19F347C2655FF535D89D71B004C#fndtn-contents">very few exceptions</a>, roses were offered to commend male medieval rulers, often ones who had militarily defended Catholicism.</p>

<p>The early modern period saw <a href="https://theconversation.com/the-lasting-impact-of-luthers-reformation-4-essential-reads-105953">the birth of the Protestant Reformation</a> and many religious conflicts. Popes looked for support from the era’s powerful women rulers, such as <a href="https://www.historyatlas.com/people/catherine-de-medici/">Catherine de’ Medici</a>, who played a crucial role during France’s wars of religion between Protestants and Catholics. From the 16th century onward, roses were often given to women like her: empresses, queens and the wives of high dignitaries.</p>

<p>That shift accelerated in the 18th and 19th centuries, when most roses were gifted to Catholic women of high standing. From 1790 to 1893 not a single man received the rose. </p>

<p>This was a period of revolutions and secularization, when the church could not depend on the military leadership of a king, duke or the nobility. Again, <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/1923/05/13/archives/popes-gold-rose-for-queens-victoria-of-spain-gets-one-king-henry.html">queens and empresses</a> dominated the beneficiaries. With the rose, popes could flatter and honor the wives of important rulers, who in turn could pressure their spouses if needed. <a href="https://www.napoleon.org/en/history-of-the-two-empires/objects/rosary-and-prayer-book-belonging-to-empress-eugenie/">Eugénie, empress of the French</a> and wife of Napoleon III, received it in 1856 for her piety and philanthropy.</p>

<figure class="align-left zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763517/original/file-20261001-60-ds640p.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A black and white portrait of a woman in a black dress and pearls." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763517/original/file-20261001-60-ds640p.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=237&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763517/original/file-20261001-60-ds640p.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=830&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763517/original/file-20261001-60-ds640p.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=830&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763517/original/file-20261001-60-ds640p.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=830&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763517/original/file-20261001-60-ds640p.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1043&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763517/original/file-20261001-60-ds640p.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1043&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763517/original/file-20261001-60-ds640p.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1043&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Charlotte, the grand duchess of Luxembourg, received a rose in 1956.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Charlotte,_Grand_Duchess_of_Luxembourg.jpg">Library of Congress via Wikimedia Commons</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>The 20th and 21st centuries saw a total abandonment of gifting the rose to humans. Instead, popes have presented them to <a href="https://www.vaticannews.va/en/pope/news/2023-12/pope-immaculate-conception-gift-golden-rose-salus-populi-romani.html">shrines and basilicas</a>, typically ones dedicated to the Virgin Mary. The last person given a rose was Charlotte, <a href="https://monarchie.lu/en/luxembourg-monarchy/former-sovereigns/hrh-grand-duchess-charlotte">grand duchess of Luxembourg</a>, who received one in 1956 for her piety and courage during World War II.</p>

<h2>1,000 years of change</h2>

<p>Today, <a href="https://www.ncregister.com/cna/pope-leo-xiv-honors-our-lady-of-almudena-with-golden-rose-reflects-on-spain-s-christian-heritage">Leo XIV</a> <a href="https://aleteia.org/2026/09/09/pope-celebrated-marys-birthday-with-good-counsel-devotion/">continues the tradition</a>. Devotion to Mary remains central to Catholic identity in an age when political authority no longer carries the same religious weight. Gifting the roses to holy shrines, images or basilicas separates them from any suggestion of political and religious alliance or favoritism.</p>

<p>The history of the golden rose reveals the shift of papal priorities from political alliance-building <a href="https://livingchurch.org/covenant/pope-francis-and-the-power-of-the-symbolic/">to devotional symbolism</a>. What was once a diplomatic gift addressed to earthly power is now offered to Marian shrines: the roses embody faith itself. The recipients changed because <a href="https://theconversation.com/trumps-clash-with-the-pope-reenacts-a-1-000-year-old-question-what-happens-when-sacred-and-secular-power-collide-280548">the church’s relationship to power changed</a>.</p>

<p>I see the rose as a perfect example of the Catholic Church’s deep understanding and adaptation to its time and its gift for reinvention. Few institutions have managed to keep a medieval ceremony alive for nearly a millennium while completely transforming its meaning. The golden rose is the papacy’s oldest public relations tool.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/293311/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

The rose is now in the Musée de Cluny, a museum of medieval art in Paris
Miguel Hermoso Cuesta/Wikimedia Commons , CC BY-SA Almost every ceremonial object or ornament of the medieval papal monarchy has disappeared or lost its original purpose
On Sept. 26, 2026, during Pope Leo XIV’s visit to France, he traveled to Lourdes, home to one of the world’s most famous shrines to the Virgin Mary
After praying, Leo presented a golden rose to Our Lady of Lourdes – the fifth time he has dedicated a rose to a Marian shrine or image
The ornate rose Leo offered to Lourdes is not that different from its medieval iterations
The oldest surviving rose is now at the Musée de Cluny in Paris and dates from the early 1300s
Both are golden, with several branches and buds
Pope Leo XIV offered a golden rose in Lourdes as part of a four-day trip to France
Yet who receives the roses, and why, has changed dramatically
As a medieval historian researching the papacy, I frequently find mentions of the roses
They are ubiquitous in medieval chronicles – most of all, in papal accounting registers
The history of the roses’ beneficiaries reflects the history of the papacy and how its influence has shifted over the centuries
Roots of tradition Most medieval roses were made of gold and silver, adorned with precious stones such as sapphires and rubies
One of the buds formed a small receptacle that held some musk and balsam , rare and expensive fragrances
The Vatican Apostolic Archives have preserved the accounting registers that itemized many of the roses’ costs
On average, they weighed 11-16 ounces of precious metal and cost the equivalent of 10 years of a laborer’s annual wage
The golden rose first appeared during the papacy of Leo IX
On April 18, 1049, the pope exempted a nunnery in Alsace – now in Sainte-Croix-en-Plaine, France – from the legal authority and supervision of the local bishop
In return, the head of the nunnery was required to offer the pope a golden rose of some 2 ounces, or of equivalent value
At the time, roses were often used to symbolize a feudal pledge : the submission of a vassal to a lord
Within a couple of generations, the gift had changed direction: The pope now granted a rose
The first clearly documented case took place in 1096, when Urban II, touring France and preaching the First Crusade, granted it to Fulk of Anjou to reward him for his willingness to participate
A 13th-century illustration of a pope bestowing a golden rose on Laetare Sunday

Musée de Cluny via Wikimedia Commons From the 11th century on, the pope offered a rose once a year, on Laetare Sunday : the fourth Sunday of Lent, the period before Easter when many Catholics commit to some form of penance
According to ceremonial books called “ordines ,” the pope held the rose during the worship service, preached about its symbolism, and presented it to a recipient
On that Sunday, gifting the rose reminded believers that while Lent was difficult, beauty and joy would emerge from it
The day was also a feast in honor of the recipient – typically the prefect of Rome , who supervised the city’s jurisdictions and police
Diplomatic tool Eventually, the decision about who should receive the honor rested solely with the pope
Still, it was always bestowed upon those who wielded power: the prefect of Rome, emperors, kings, military leaders and defenders of Christian lands
Receiving the rose was a public acknowledgment that the recipient – usually a warrior – stood beside the pope in protecting the church
In 1148, for example, Pope Eugene III offered it to the king of Leon and Castile , Alfonso VII
A century later, Pope Innocent IV gave it to Raymond Berenger , count of Provence
In both cases the pope rewarded the fight against Muslims, whom the Vatican saw as “infidels” or heretics
The Avignon papacy of the 14th century, a period when several popes resided in what is now southern France, accelerated this evolution
Away from Rome, and in the absence of a Roman prefect, the rose’s role as a negotiating tool intensified
By the 14th century, the ceremony had grown even more elaborate
According to ceremonial books, the pope carried the rose in procession, while its beneficiary held the reins of his horse and kissed the pope’s feet – a gesture of submission

<title>2026 midterms could be the end of Pennsylvania’s split legislature, with effects on affordability, election reform, marijuana and more</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763495/original/file-20261001-50-opht6n.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=8%2C0%2C6821%2C4547&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Pennsylvania voters could shift the balance of power in Harrisburg in the 2026 midterms.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/fresh-sheet-of-i-voted-stickers-sits-ready-to-be-news-photo/2276547221">Matthew Hatcher/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>While many people are paying attention to how the 2026 midterm elections might change the balance of power in Washington, D.C., it is also a potentially pivotal election here in Pennsylvania. </p>

<p>Gov. Josh Shapiro is up for reelection, running against Republican challenger Stacy Garrity, the current state treasurer. Who wins that race will certainly shape the state’s policy agenda for the next two years. </p>

<p>In the General Assembly, which is <a href="https://theconversation.com/pennsylvania-will-keep-its-divided-legislature-thanks-to-split-ticket-voters-243187">currently split</a> – Republicans control the Senate and Democrats control the House – both chambers are also up for grabs. Democrats have been slowly eroding the <a href="https://www.spotlightpa.org/news/2026/09/races-to-watch-pennsylvania-house-senate-2026-midterm-election-elections/">Republicans’ hold over the Senate</a>. In the House, Democrats have a three-seat majority, but <a href="https://politicspa.com/election-2026-the-state-house-races-were-watching/153143/">Republicans could flip it</a>. </p>

<p>Of course, nationally the <a href="https://www.fandmpoll.org/franklin-marshall-college-poll-release-pa-7th-and-10th-congressional-districts-september-2026/">wind is at the back of Democrats</a>. Commentators are contemplating the possibility of a Democratic trifecta in Pennsylvania <a href="https://ballotpedia.org/Party_control_of_Pennsylvania_state_government">for the first time since 1993</a>. </p>

<p>I teach public policy at Penn State Harrisburg and have a particular interest in <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=NE3FeMgAAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=ao">Pennsylvania state politics</a>. I think voters should understand not just the positions of the individual candidates on the ballot, but what the legislative priorities will be for either party if they gain control of the General Assembly. </p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="A man in suit and tie speaks at podium" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763496/original/file-20261001-50-isbklv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763496/original/file-20261001-50-isbklv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=398&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763496/original/file-20261001-50-isbklv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=398&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763496/original/file-20261001-50-isbklv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=398&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763496/original/file-20261001-50-isbklv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=500&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763496/original/file-20261001-50-isbklv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=500&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763496/original/file-20261001-50-isbklv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=500&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, a Democrat, works with a split legislature, with Republicans controlling the Senate and Democrats controlling the House.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/pennsylvania-gov-josh-shapiro-delivers-the-keynote-speech-news-photo/2295192931">Jeff Swensen/Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>If Democrats control the Assembly</h2>

<p>For a glimpse at potential Democratic priorities should they keep the House and win the Senate, it is helpful to look at what legislation the current Democrat-controlled House <a href="https://www.pahouse.com/deliveringforpa">has been sending the</a> Republican-controlled Senate. </p>

<p><strong>1. Election reform</strong></p>

<p>Election reform has been a perennial priority in the commonwealth since the passage of <a href="https://www.palegis.us/statutes/consolidated/view-statute?SESSYR=2019&amp;SESSIND=0&amp;ACTNUM=0077.&amp;CHPT=000.&amp;SCTN=000.&amp;SUBSCTN=000.">Act 77 of 2019</a> and the 2020 election. Act 77 authorized no-excuse absentee balloting and eliminated straight-ticket voting, which was <a href="https://www.northcentralpa.com/news/historic-election-reform-bill-including-new-mail-in-voting-signed/article_f11a1a06-fcb9-11e9-b1f5-1b9c92f767de.html">a bipartisan compromise</a> but became a political flash point in President Donald Trump’s efforts to question the 2020 election results. No-excuse means that voters do not need to provide a specific qualifying reason to vote by mail.</p>

<p>Democratic election law priorities have included requiring counties to <a href="https://www.votebeat.org/pennsylvania/2025/05/13/voting-election-legislation-voter-identification-mail-ballot-precanvassing/">use ballot drop boxes</a>, maintaining <a href="https://www.democracydocket.com/news-alerts/democrats-seek-to-defend-mail-in-voting-from-gop-attack-in-pennsylvania/">no-excuse mail-in voting</a>, setting clear rules for <a href="https://www.votebeat.org/pennsylvania/2025/05/13/voting-election-legislation-voter-identification-mail-ballot-precanvassing/">ballot curing</a>, instituting <a href="https://www.votebeat.org/pennsylvania/2025/05/13/voting-election-legislation-voter-identification-mail-ballot-precanvassing/">precanvassing</a> to speed the counting of absentee ballots, and allowing independents to vote in <a href="https://www.spotlightpa.org/news/2026/09/pennsylvania-state-house-passes-open-primaries-bill-harrisburg-elections/">open primary elections</a>.</p>

<p><strong>2. Marijuana</strong></p>

<p>Gov. Shapiro has repeatedly included revenue projections from adult-use recreational marijuana legalization in his budget proposals, and the House even <a href="https://www.mpp.org/states/pennsylvania/">passed a legalization bill in 2025</a>. Democrats have said that <a href="https://whyy.org/articles/pennsylvania-adult-use-marijuana-november-election/">they will legalize recreational marijuana</a> if they can take the Senate in 2026. But important details of legalization will remain to be worked out, even if Democrats have full control. </p>

<p>Democrats and Republican supporters of legalization disagree as to whether sales should be through private dispensaries or <a href="https://theconversation.com/as-pennsylvania-inches-toward-legalizing-recreational-cannabis-lawmakers-propose-selling-it-in-state-owned-dispensaries-similar-to-state-liquor-stores-250368">state stores</a>, similar to how alcohol is sold in Pennsylvania. </p>

<p>Social equity measures meant to repair some of the harms of the War on Drugs on communities disproportionately affected by the criminalization of marijuana will also be key to eventual passage. These include things like expungements of past convictions, license set-asides for minority dispensary owners, and community reinvestment of cannabis tax revenues. Even with Democratic control, the devil will be in the details. </p>

<p><strong>3. Same-sex marriage</strong></p>

<p>Same-sex marriage equality may seem like a settled issue with the 2015 <a href="https://www.oyez.org/cases/2014/14-556">Obergefell v. Hodges decision</a> by the U.S. Supreme Court, but the 2022 <a href="https://www.oyez.org/cases/2021/19-1392">overturning</a> of <a href="https://www.oyez.org/cases/1971/70-18">Roe v. Wade</a> by today’s more conservative court has sparked concerns of further changes to precedent. </p>

<p>Pennsylvania’s statutory definition of marriage is still between “one man and one woman,” something that a bipartisan majority in the House <a href="https://www.palegis.us/legislation/bills/2025/hb1800">tried to change in 2026</a> to “two individuals.”  Democrats are very likely to pick this back up if they win a trifecta. They may even attempt a more durable, but also <a href="https://ballotpedia.org/Pennsylvania_Constitution">more procedurally difficult</a>, constitutional amendment that enshrines same-sex marriage rights. </p>

<p><strong>4. Data centers and AI</strong></p>

<p>The House has passed several measures to regulate AI and the data center build-out in the commonwealth. This includes a measure that would <a href="https://www.palegis.us/legislation/bills/2025/hb0095">require warnings</a> on advertisements that were made using AI and several that target <a href="https://www.palegis.us/legislation/bills/2025/hb1834">energy costs</a>, <a href="https://www.palegis.us/legislation/bills/2025/hb2246">water use</a>, <a href="https://www.palegis.us/legislation/bills/2025/hb2496">local government authority</a> and <a href="https://www.palegis.us/legislation/bills/2025/hb2650">implementing</a> the <a href="https://www.spotlightpa.org/news/2026/08/pennsylvania-data-center-executive-order-shapiro-explainer-environment/">Governor’s Responsible Infrastructure Development</a> plan. These measures and others are likely to remain on the Democrats’ agenda. </p>

<p><strong>5. Affordability</strong></p>

<p>Given that this election is shaping up to be heavily influenced by <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2026/0/as-the-2026-midterms-approach-economy-is-front-and-center/">voters’ concerns about affordability</a>, both parties have the issue on their agendas but will approach it differently. </p>

<p>The Democrats’ <a href="https://pasenate.com/affordability/">Affordability Action Plan</a> includes measures such as property tax and rent rebates, other housing protections for underserved communities, doubling the income tax credit and increasing food and energy security funding.</p>

<p>Another affordability priority for House Democrats since taking control of the chamber in 2023 has been raising the state’s US$7.25 minimum hourly wage over time. The <a href="https://www.palegis.us/legislation/bills/2025/hb2189">bill passed by the House</a> in March 2026 would have raised it to $11 in 2027, $13 in 2028 and $15 in 2029, with subsequent annual cost-of-living adjustments, if it had been also passed by the Senate. This is important in Philadelphia, given that <a href="https://www.nbcphiladelphia.com/news/politics/philly-doesnt-have-the-authority-to-raise-its-minimum-wage-heres-why/3530750/">state law prohibits</a> the city from setting its own minimum wage.</p>

<figure class="align-center ">

<h2>If Republicans control the Assembly</h2>

<p>We can turn to the current Republican-controlled Senate for insight into what will be on the party’s agenda if it resumes full control of the Assembly in 2027. </p>

<p><strong>1. Election reform</strong></p>

<p>Republicans have also been pushing for election law reform since 2020. In contrast to Democrats, their agenda has included repealing <a href="https://www.npr.org/2022/08/02/1099806224/pennsylvania-act-77-supreme-court-decision-mail-in-voting-lawsuit">no-excuse absentee balloting</a>, banning the <a href="https://penncapital-star.com/government-politics/the-ballots-are-called-mail-in-ballots-pa-senate-approves-bill-eliminating-drop-boxes/">use of ballot drop boxes</a> and instituting <a href="https://www.pasenategop.com/news/pennycuick-to-introduce-voter-id-measure/">stronger voter identification</a> requirements. </p>

<p><strong>2. Data centers and AI</strong></p>

<p>Senate Republicans have also been active in proposing and passing AI- and data center-related legislation. A bill banning “nudification” apps, which use AI to remove the clothing from people in pictures and replace them with fake nude images, <a href="https://www.pasenategop.com/news/pennycuick-bipartisan-legislation-to-ban-nudification-apps-passes-senate/">passed the Senate</a> unanimously in late September.</p>

<p>There has also been <a href="https://www.abc27.com/pa-data-centers/bill-to-ban-ndas-between-data-center-developers-municipalities-unanimously-passes-committee/">bipartisan support</a> for a Republican-proposed ban on the use of nondisclosure agreements in data center development. Republicans in the Senate also proposed designating all of Pennsylvania a <a href="https://www.palegis.us/senate/co-sponsorship/memo?memoID=47094&amp;document=SB939">Commonwealth Opportunity Zone</a> for AI, which would fast-track data center permits and create a regulatory framework in collaboration with the industry. </p>

<p>While Republican AI legislation is likely to be more enabling of the emergent industry than regulating, Republicans are also concerned about privacy, transparency and costs to their constituents. </p>

<p><strong>3. Energy</strong></p>

<p>Among the costs of data center development are <a href="https://theconversation.com/why-your-electricity-bill-is-so-high-and-what-pennsylvania-is-doing-about-it-254562">higher energy</a> and <a href="https://theconversation.com/how-pennsylvania-towns-are-protecting-themselves-from-the-noise-heat-and-utility-costs-of-massive-data-centers-282126">water prices</a>. Republicans have already been making energy development a priority, repealing Pennsylvania’s <a href="https://www.wesanews.org/politics-government/2025-11-18/pittman-topper-greenhouse-gas-initiative-repeal">participation in the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative</a> and pushing the governor on his promise of an “<a href="https://www.abc27.com/spotlight-pa/pa-election-2026-where-governor-candidates-garrity-and-shapiro-stand-on-energy-costs-the-environment-and-more/">all of the above</a>” energy strategy. </p>

<p>The stark promise of higher electric prices and poorer grid reliability due to projected data center development in a <a href="https://www.puc.pa.gov/press-release/2026/puc-study-warns-rapid-data-center-growth-could-pose-serious-risks-to-electric-reliability-09142026">2026 Public Utility Commission report</a> is likely to add fuel to Republicans’ push for energy development.  </p>

<p><strong>4. Affordability</strong></p>

<p>The affordability plan <a href="https://www.pahousegop.com/News/37743/Latest-News/PA-House-Republicans-Launch-Freedom-Through-Affordability-Initiative-to-Cut-Costs-for-Families">released by House Republicans in March 2026</a> points to the types of measures the party will pursue if it takes control of the Assembly. A cornerstone is the <a href="https://www.facebook.com/pahousegop/videos/1547903920001214/">reduction of taxes</a>, including lowering the personal income tax rate, a temporary elimination of energy and telecommunications taxes, and suspending the state gas tax, which is <a href="https://www.pa.gov/agencies/revenue/resources/tax-rates/motor-fuel-tax-rates">$0.576 per gallon for gasoline, $0.741 for diesel</a>. Pennsylvania’s gasoline tax is the <a href="https://taxfoundation.org/data/all/state/gas-taxes-state/">fifth-highest</a> and the diesel tax is the <a href="https://taxfoundation.org/data/all/state/gas-taxes-state/">third-highest</a> in the United States.</p>

<p>A full plan with 10 bills <a href="https://pennbizreport.com/news/33462-house-gop-previews-pa-affordability-package/">is to be released in coming weeks</a>, but will also include changes to zoning and construction rules to enable faster housing construction.</p>

body: Pennsylvania voters could shift the balance of power in Harrisburg in the 2026 midterms

Matthew Hatcher/Getty Images While many people are paying attention to how the 2026 midterm elections might change the balance of power in Washington, D.C., it is also a potentially pivotal election here in Pennsylvania
Josh Shapiro is up for reelection, running against Republican challenger Stacy Garrity, the current state treasurer
Who wins that race will certainly shape the state’s policy agenda for the next two years
In the General Assembly, which is currently split – Republicans control the Senate and Democrats control the House – both chambers are also up for grabs
Democrats have been slowly eroding the Republicans’ hold over the Senate
In the House, Democrats have a three-seat majority, but Republicans could flip it
Of course, nationally the wind is at the back of Democrats
Commentators are contemplating the possibility of a Democratic trifecta in Pennsylvania for the first time since 1993
I teach public policy at Penn State Harrisburg and have a particular interest in Pennsylvania state politics

I think voters should understand not just the positions of the individual candidates on the ballot, but what the legislative priorities will be for either party if they gain control of the General Assembly
Josh Shapiro, a Democrat, works with a split legislature, with Republicans controlling the Senate and Democrats controlling the House

Jeff Swensen/Getty Images If Democrats control the Assembly For a glimpse at potential Democratic priorities should they keep the House and win the Senate, it is helpful to look at what legislation the current Democrat-controlled House has been sending the Republican-controlled Senate. 1
Election reform Election reform has been a perennial priority in the commonwealth since the passage of Act 77 of 2019 and the 2020 election

Act 77 authorized no-excuse absentee balloting and eliminated straight-ticket voting, which was a bipartisan compromise but became a political flash point in President Donald Trump’s efforts to question the 2020 election results
No-excuse means that voters do not need to provide a specific qualifying reason to vote by mail

Democratic election law priorities have included requiring counties to use ballot drop boxes , maintaining no-excuse mail-in voting , setting clear rules for ballot curing , instituting precanvassing to speed the counting of absentee ballots, and allowing independents to vote in open primary elections . 2
Shapiro has repeatedly included revenue projections from adult-use recreational marijuana legalization in his budget proposals, and the House even passed a legalization bill in 2025
Democrats have said that they will legalize recreational marijuana if they can take the Senate in 2026
But important details of legalization will remain to be worked out, even if Democrats have full control
Democrats and Republican supporters of legalization disagree as to whether sales should be through private dispensaries or state stores , similar to how alcohol is sold in Pennsylvania
Social equity measures meant to repair some of the harms of the War on Drugs on communities disproportionately affected by the criminalization of marijuana will also be key to eventual passage
These include things like expungements of past convictions, license set-asides for minority dispensary owners, and community reinvestment of cannabis tax revenues
Even with Democratic control, the devil will be in the details. 3
Same-sex marriage Same-sex marriage equality may seem like a settled issue with the 2015 Obergefell v
Supreme Court, but the 2022 overturning of Roe v
Wade by today’s more conservative court has sparked concerns of further changes to precedent

Pennsylvania’s statutory definition of marriage is still between “one man and one woman,” something that a bipartisan majority in the House tried to change in 2026 to “two individuals.” Democrats are very likely to pick this back up if they win a trifecta
They may even attempt a more durable, but also more procedurally difficult , constitutional amendment that enshrines same-sex marriage rights. 4
Data centers and AI The House has passed several measures to regulate AI and the data center build-out in the commonwealth

This includes a measure that would require warnings on advertisements that were made using AI and several that target energy costs , water use , local government authority and implementing the Governor’s Responsible Infrastructure Development plan
These measures and others are likely to remain on the Democrats’ agenda. 5
Affordability Given that this election is shaping up to be heavily influenced by voters’ concerns about affordability , both parties have the issue on their agendas but will approach it differently

The Democrats’ Affordability Action Plan includes measures such as property tax and rent rebates, other housing protections for underserved communities, doubling the income tax credit and increasing food and energy security funding
Another affordability priority for House Democrats since taking control of the chamber in 2023 has been raising the state’s US$7.25 minimum hourly wage over time

The bill passed by the House in March 2026 would have raised it to $11 in 2027, $13 in 2028 and $15 in 2029, with subsequent annual cost-of-living adjustments, if it had been also passed by the Senate
This is important in Philadelphia, given that state law prohibits the city from setting its own minimum wage
Communities across the state are pushing back against large data centers
