title: Trump’s plan to buy votes, briefly explained
excerpt: President Donald Trump speaks on stage at the Butler-Vandalia Student Activity Center on October 3, 2026, in Vandalia, Ohio. | Roberto Schmidt/Getty Images This
body: President Donald Trump speaks on stage at the Butler-Vandalia Student Activity Center on October 3, 2026, in Vandalia, Ohio. | Roberto Schmidt/Getty Images This story appeared in  The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life.  Subscribe here

Welcome to The Logoff: Donald Trump is trying to bribe his way out of a midterm disaster.  What’s happening? Over the weekend, Trump announced a plan to send $90 payments to more than 20 million Americans 65 years and older, drawing from a pool of money called the Medicare Improvement Fund.  Trump, in a post, described the payments as part of a strategy to “substantially LOWER costs for our Seniors” — but the money, a single nonrecurring payment set to go out this month, was reportedly already earmarked for other programs before Trump decided to redirect it.  Why now? Trump, facing a potentially catastrophic midterms for his party, has been looking for any way to turn out (Republican) voters — up to and including offering them cash, either implicitly or explicitly, in return for their support.  In the implicit category: these $90 payments and a smaller number of $500 Affordable Care Act refunds (fewer than 1 million) that began going out last week.  Much more explicitly, however, he’s also promising Americans $5,000 if they reelect Republicans in the midterms

Trump has directly linked Medicare payments with the promised checks: “Because I delivered on this very important issue for the American People,” he wrote in a post, “they can also rest assured the highly popular $5,000 Trump Dividend will be distributed to every U.S

Citizen if, and when, the Republicans win the Midterm Elections!” Will it work? It’s hard to say for sure, but it feels unlikely: The Medicare payments are relatively small, while the ACA payments are going out to relatively few voters

Polling suggests that voters are not fans of the promised $5,000 checks, and even fewer believe that they’re going to happen (they’re almost certainly correct ).  What else should I know? Direct payments to Americans — real or promised — are not the only way Trump is trying to sway the midterms in his favor
He’s also continuing to spend taxpayer dollars on a propagandistic ad campaign , which he personally directed

And with that, it’s time to log off… Vox’s Unexplainable podcast team is back with a deeply controversial new question: What color are tennis balls? Personally, I think yellow, but whatever your opinion, it’s a fascinating conversation
You can listen here , or read a partial transcript here
Thanks for reading, have a great evening, and we’ll see you tomorrow!

title: What you should know about the Russian “plague lab”
excerpt: People stroll along the river in Irkutsk, Russia, where the recent death of a lab technician prompted quarantines. | Hao Jianwei/Xinhua via Getty Images This st
body: People stroll along the river in Irkutsk, Russia, where the recent death of a lab technician prompted quarantines. | Hao Jianwei/Xinhua via Getty Images This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day

The death of a 28-year-old lab tech halfway around the world is not typically the sort of thing the White House monitors .  But when that tech dies of severe pneumonia…while working at a Siberian plague research lab…foreign governments (and pretty much everyone in my timeline) tend to pay more attention.   The World Health Organization says that there’s little cause for concern , to be clear
Testing has turned up no connection between the woman’s work and her cause of death.  And even if she did contract pneumonic plague, that’s hardly a doomsday scenario
The plague comes in three flavors — bubonic, septicemic, and pneumonic — and they all crop up from time to time, particularly in places like Central Asia and Africa
If caught early, pneumonic plague is typically curable with common antibiotics

A man in Arizona caught the disease from his cat in 2025 , for instance, but didn’t spread it to anyone else.  Of course, the real fear (and the reason so many people are talking about this today, I suspect) is that Russia has, at various times in its history, worked to develop more deadly and contagious forms of plague for use as a biological weapon.  There’s no evidence linking that program to this lab or this death in Siberia
Still, the general threat of biological warfare is so ominous and urgent that now seems like a worthwhile time to understand it a bit better

Go a little deeper In her very recent and slightly spooky book, Biological War: A Scenario,  journalist Annie Jacobsen lays out how world governments and health authorities are poised to respond to the hypothetical leak of a weaponized pneumonic plague from a Russian lab
At the risk of being euphemistic here, let me say that she concludes things would not go well.  But wait! There’s even more doom and gloom where that thought experiment came from

AI chatbots have made it hypothetically possible for more-or-less ordinary people to grasp the research and techniques they’d need to hack together their own biological weapons.  Just last month, the AI giant Anthropic disclosed five cases where scientists had tried to use its software on research that could have been used in weapons development
And while the company apparently shut those attempts down, their mere existence is fairly frightening
Can anything be done about these risks, now that they’re here? My colleague Noel King asked Jacobsen that very question in early September
Jacobsen essentially said that the public needs to demand policies aimed at avoiding the “nightmare scenario,” whether that’s an inadvertent lab leak or terrorist attack
Such policies might include things like independent testing of AI models or stricter licensing requirements for high-risk labs.  But it’s unclear what authority could rein in bad state-level actors
And it’s hard to imagine a public upswell for such niche scientific regulations, particularly at a moment when we don’t lack for other doomsday threats
For now, I suppose, I’ll take (partial, provisional) solace in the fact that this Russian situation doesn’t look like one of them.  One link for later ➨ Curtail your catastrophizing

Catastrophizing is a common thought pattern where you assume the worst possible scenario. (For instance, perhaps you read about a quarantine in Russia and began to fear for the end of the world!) Catastrophic thinking can help prepare us for difficult or frightening situations, but it can also be a major source of stress

Try interrogating your doomsday thoughts and noting when the worst case doesn’t come to pass.  Before you go… Did you know… that, according to some physicists, glass defies categorization as a simple liquid, solid, or gas ? It looks like a solid, but its molecular structure is more like a liquid.  Today’s trivia: Between 1968 and 1973, the British government forcibly removed the native inhabitants from which Indian Ocean island? (You can find this and other brain puzzles in Vox’s daily crossword
Look for the answer in tomorrow’s edition.) Yesterday’s trivia: Last week we asked you what musical note is equivalent to a G sharp

title: The Supreme Court is looking for a way to kill climate lawsuits
excerpt: Justice Neil Gorsuch and Chief Justice John Roberts. | Win McNamee/Getty Images Inside Chief Justice John Roberts are two wolves
body: Justice Neil Gorsuch and Chief Justice John Roberts. | Win McNamee/Getty Images Inside Chief Justice John Roberts are two wolves
The first wolf is a staunch conservative who spent much of his career litigating on behalf of corporate interests
This wolf looks at a series of climate change lawsuits that could potentially cost the oil industry billions of dollars or more, and recoils in horror
The second wolf is a judge tasked with following the law wherever it leads
And that wolf seemed baffled by the oil industry’s arguments in Suncor Energy v
County Commissioners of Boulder County , a Supreme Court case where two oil companies are asking the justices to shut down dozens of climate change lawsuits
The Court’s decision in Suncor is likely to shape the future of climate litigation in the United States

If the oil industry prevails, that will probably shut down climate change-related suits in state courts — and it may shut them down entirely because it is unclear whether federal law allows these suits to proceed in federal court
If the oil industry loses, by contrast, it could face dozens of suits in state courts across the country seeking billions of dollars or more
And the outcome in Suncor is likely to turn on which wolf shows up to the justices’ conference on how to decide the case
Roberts, who asked the most ambiguous questions at Monday’s oral argument in Suncor , clearly wants these lawsuits to disappear
But he also appeared doubtful that the oil companies’ weak legal arguments will allow him to make that disappearing act happen
Notably, Justice Samuel Alito, who owns stock in oil and gas companies , is recused from hearing the case
So, in the likely event that all three of the Court’s Democrats hold together against the oil companies, Roberts would split the Court 4-4 if he decides to join them
That would leave the Court unable to render a decision, and a lower court opinion, which rejected the oil companies’ bid for lawsuit immunity, would remain in effect
That said, at least two other justices asked questions suggesting that their votes may potentially be in play
Justice Clarence Thomas, who otherwise appeared sympathetic to the oil companies, repeatedly asked whether his Court has jurisdiction to hear Suncor in the first place

Meanwhile, while most of Democratic Justice Elena Kagan’s questions seemed to favor allowing the climate change lawsuits to proceed, she did ask some questions at the end that indicated that she may be looking for a narrow reason to hand the oil companies a win
The bottom line is that it is difficult to predict how this case will turn out, as more than one justice asked questions that suggest that their vote is, at least, in play
But the outcome is likely to hinge upon the tension within Roberts — who both signaled that he wants the oil companies to win, but who also expressed deep skepticism of their primary legal argument

So what is Suncor actually about? Suncor is one of many lawsuits brought by state or local governments (in this case, the plaintiff is Boulder, Colorado) who’ve sued oil companies claiming that those companies should be liable for the harms caused by climate change within those governments’ jurisdictions

In this particular case, the defendants are Exxon Mobil and Suncor, a company that operates two oil refineries in Colorado.  The lawyer for these two companies, Kannon Shanmugam, told the justices that there are about 60 similar cases brought by municipal governments throughout the country

And, in one of his more pro-oil moments during Monday’s oral argument, Roberts predicted that if Boulder wins in the Supreme Court, there will be numerous other copycat lawsuits filed by other municipalities
The question in Suncor is whether state courts, including Colorado’s own courts, are forbidden from hearing these sorts of climate change lawsuits

As Roberts pointed out in one of his less pro-oil moments during Monday’s argument, “there are a lot of familiar situations where conduct outside of a state has broad effects on other states…and yet we allow the state courts in a particular state to bring litigation.” He pointed to “mass tort” suits and “complaints about operations of the internet” as two examples where state courts hear lawsuits involving harms that arise across state borders
The oil companies’ primary argument is that suits involving air and water pollution are special
But their evidence supporting this argument is confusing and difficult to parse .  Briefly, the oil companies point to several cases, many of which were decided more than a century ago
These cases held that, before Congress enacted the Clean Air Act in 1963, states could sometimes sue other states for cross-border pollution, even though no federal law forbade such pollution
The Supreme Court created “federal common law” permitting these suits, and the oil companies claim that this federal common law preempted any state lawsuits that covered a similar subject matter

This federal common law, they now argue, has itself been displaced by the Clear Air Act and its partner statute, the Clean Water Act, but the principle that state suits involving air and water pollution are preempted is somehow still in effect

Although there is no provision in the text of the Constitution that supports this argument by the oil companies, those companies claim that their argument is implicit in the “ structure of the Constitution .” The oil companies’ primary legal argument is difficult to understand If you are confused by all the arcane history and logical leaps contained in the oil companies’ argument, don’t worry
Only Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who repeatedly claimed that his Court’s precedents bar Boulder’s lawsuit, seemed to buy what the oil companies are saying without reservation
Most of the other justices expressed at least some reservations

Justice Amy Coney Barrett, for example, argued that even under the older “federal common law” regime, states still retained some authority over environmental lawsuits, although she noted that the Court’s previous decisions do not really define the scope of that authority
Kagan pointed out that the many suits challenging climate change are similar to past litigation against tobacco and opioid manufacturers
But those suits were heard by state courts
Many of the justices appear bothered that these lawsuits exist, but the most skeptical justices couldn’t agree on a legal theory they could use to shut them down

It seems unlikely, in other words, that there are five votes for the oil companies’ convoluted claim that the “structure of the Constitution” somehow bars state courts from hearing climate change lawsuits

But several of the justices did appear troubled by what could happen if dozens of state courts reach conflicting judgments on who is responsible for climate change and who should receive compensation because of it

And some of these justices floated alternative theories for how to hand the oil companies a win.  At one point, for example, Barrett floated the possibility that, if the plaintiffs lose in Suncor , they might file a new suit under the now-defunct federal common law that existed prior to the Clean Air Act

title: What color is a tennis ball?
excerpt: A while back, I was at physical therapy, and the topic of tennis came up
body: A while back, I was at physical therapy, and the topic of tennis came up

Someone said something about yellow tennis balls, and I was like… “What? They’re green.” And then someone else chimed in, “No, they’re yellow!” And then someone across the room hollered, “No, they’re obviously green.” There was basically a physical therapy uproar
And when I started asking other people how they saw them — yellow or green — they told me they couldn’t even believe there was a debate
He’s a neuroscientist who heads up a lab at the National Eye Institute
He’s working on a book called Color Coded , which is due out next year
And he’s also a working artist — which is actually how he got into studying color in the first place.  Conway told me there’s a pretty good reason for why so many people disagree about tennis balls

He said it’s simple: “There’s no such thing as a color.” In the latest episode of Unexplainable , I talked with Conway about what color even is , the viral dress fight (black and blue or white and gold?), and why we get so upset when people don’t see color the same way we do
Below is an excerpt of our conversation, edited for length and clarity
Listen to the episode anywhere you get your podcasts or you can watch on Netflix
You’re also working on a book about color
Are there still color mysteries? Are there things science doesn’t know about color?  There are lots of mysteries about color

For a long time, people thought that color was a little bit like a filter, that everything that’s really important is in black and white, and then there’s a color filter you put on top of it.  But a bunch of years ago, my lab were blown away to discover that there’s as much brain involved in processing color as there is in face recognition

The same amount of processing power? Yeah, there’s tons and tons of tissue [and] pretty fancy bits of brain that are doing pretty high-level things — parts of brain we think of as being involved in social cognition and in high-level reasoning and visual memory
Color must be more than just this little add-on
So we’re trying to understand what those bits of brain are doing

So what is color? How does it work? How do our brains and eyes perceive it?  The classic definition would be: Color is the visual feature that you get from wavelength properties of the light entering your eye
People typically see the long wavelength end as red light, and then going through short wavelengths, you know, following ROYGBIV: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet
If color were just wavelength, then an object under blue light would look blue, and the same object under yellow light would look yellow
And that wouldn’t be very helpful — because what you want is a signal that tells you about objects, immune to the lighting condition
You want them to always have that color.  A perfect example is a peach
If you look at a peach outside and you look at it inside, it’s always gonna look like a peach color
But if you looked at the pattern of wavelengths that are coming off of the peach, they’re very different under different lighting conditions
They should be different colors if color were just wavelength, but they’re not

Those two different compositions of wavelengths look the same color.  What I think is so cool about color is it’s so fundamental for how we need to experience the world — but the mechanics of how it does it teaches us a lot about the brain
What we’re talking about is color constancy

That is, an object’s color is constant despite the viewing conditions.  So if the peach is fundamentally a different color inside and outside, and our brains are telling us that it is still, you know, peach colored, how are our brains deceiving us?    So it’s not fundamentally a different color
The problem is that you are carrying around, Noam, in your head an idea that color is wavelength, and that is the mistake
Color is not wavelength! And we’ve known this for a long time

But the problem is that we want something that is an empirical, measurable number that’s outside of an observer, that’s a thing out there in the world, that would be the same number regardless of who looks at it
And color, at its core, is not that.  Color is dependent on your own visual system interacting with the world
And that doesn’t mean it’s any less real
It just means that its reality is dependent on psychological neural brain processes
And that’s what makes color fascinating.  Color is, you’re saying, something that is essentially created in the brain.  Absolutely, yes
Color is a generative product of the brain that gives us reliable, useful, true, meaningful, objective information, but it itself is not [those things]
It’s some generative product of your brain in order to come up with this information that’s useful and meaningful about the world. [Your brain is] actually creating that thing that is a color

Colors don’t exist out there in the world independent of a viewer to see them.  Is this related to “the dress” — you know, like 10 years ago when that photo of a dress went viral, and a bunch of people on the internet thought it was blue and black, and a bunch of other people thought it was white and gold, and everyone got super upset ? Is this the same type of thing, of seeing something in different lighting or different contexts and perceiving a different color?  It is

So the dress was fascinating because people with normal color vision looking at exactly the same thing were asserting very different perceptions.  And, you know, from a deep kind of philosophical point of view, it’s important because they weren’t saying, “Yeah, it kinda looks different to me, but I understand how you could see it as different.” They were like, “No, it is white and gold.” And other people were saying, “It is different colors.” That was, for me professionally and personally, a really big deal because it underscored this fact that color is this generative, constructive thing that your brain is doing, making all kinds of assumptions, filling in the gaps about lighting, about what you think you’re seeing
In the case of the dress, it’s such a crappy little photograph, very blurry
It doesn’t give you a lot of context
And your visual system, your own brain, has to make a guess about what the lighting is

title: The Senate’s new permitting plan could change how America gets energy for a generation
excerpt: Congress has a new bipartisan plan to lower your power bill. | David Paul Morris/Bloombe There’s no place like Kansas, a state whose howling winds are so fierce
body: Congress has a new bipartisan plan to lower your power bill. | David Paul Morris/Bloombe There’s no place like Kansas, a state whose howling winds are so fierce that in the 1800s, the roaring soundscape drove local farmers into madness

It is so windy in Kansas that every so often, trains get swept off their tracks or trampolines get hurled into the air and flung into neighbors’ trees.  But today, the same gusts that whisked away Dorothy’s home have made Kansas the third-most wind-powered place in the country, its great plains dotted with thousands of twirling turbines responsible for generating over half of the state’s energy.  And for years, Kansas has been trying to share.  But that’s easier said than done in the US, where building power lines across state borders can be an onerous, litigious, and bureaucratic slog
The Grain Belt Express , a proposed 800-mile high-voltage line carrying Kansas’ windy riches across Missouri, Illinois, and Indiana, has been trying to get built for the past 16 years
When completed, it will allow Kansas to pump five times as much wind power into Missouri as it does now

But though the project received its first approval in 2013, it will likely not open until 2029 at the earliest, beset by regulatory hurdles across multiple jurisdictions and an endless stream of legal challenges that immediately halt progress every time a new injunction is filed
Alas, the express — which only broke ground this year — was forced to run oh so local.  But other projects like it might soon enjoy far more reasonable timelines

On Wednesday, a bipartisan group of Senators announced a deal called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA — an acronym that’s led to a slew of cringeworthy euphoric Baja Blast references from abundance Democrats , clean energy advocates, and oil industry lobbyists alike

If passed, it would significantly curtail Americans’ ability to endlessly litigate against energy projects they don’t like, and empower the federal government to push critical multistate projects forward even if one state or municipality drags its feet

That could remake the way the nation’s energy infrastructure gets built, including its interstate transmission lines, for decades to come.  But the bill also suggests that easing the way for clean energy in the US may require simultaneously creating the conditions for more oil and gas infrastructure in a country that already has a lot of it

It would also mean defanging some of the landmark regulatory norms that for decades have, for example, given Americans a say over developments that could contaminate their drinking water and helped tribes protect sacred heritage sites

These laws were necessary in the first place because prior to the 1970s, American communities frequently found themselves both literally and figuratively steamrolled  by developers singularly focused on building things quickly with little regard for the oil spills, river fires , and bifurcated neighborhoods they left in their wake
And yet today, half a century later, that same dilemma has, in some ways, turned on its head

America builds things too slowly, and in particular, it builds the kind of infrastructure desperately needed to usher in a transition to clean energy with little of the urgency you’d expect from a world in the throes of climate change-related disaster

Exasperatingly, some of the same protections that have played a critical role in making this nation safer may also be standing in the way of building a nation that is more affordable and sustainable in the long run

There are still plenty of reasons to feel hopeful about the world’s transition away from fossil fuels, even in the US, which has lagged behind our peers while still building an extraordinary number of solar and wind farms , particularly in Republican-led states like Kansas and Texas

And yet, many of these projects have languished in never-ending Ticketmaster-esque queues to connect to the nation’s decrepit power grid, a direct result of the permitting hellscape that prevents much-needed high-voltage cables like the Grain Belt Express from coming online.       This new bill aims to ease many of the bottlenecks that stymie clean energy, but it also throws a bone to fossil fuels, which, like renewables, would benefit from less onerous environmental reviews and quicker permissions

This is, after all, a bipartisan bill in a Congress that, at least for now, remains Republican-led, under the tutelage of an aggrieved president who has sabotaged some of the nation’s most promising clean energy projects with an often petty and relentless fervor
Some Democrats in Congress , along with other environmentalists, have raised serious concerns about the bill

Those initial objections may prophesize an uphill battle for it when it comes to a vote, likely after the November midterms.  Even so, with American electricity bills spiking to frightening new heights , and a data center buildout that could all but snap the power grid in half, this ambitious deal is, at the very least, an indication that some of the nation’s representatives are finally listening

And if it passes into law in the months to come, it could very well remake how Americans get their energy for a generation.  So why are environmentalists mad? By most accounts, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act almost didn’t happen.  For months, the proposed permitting deal has been stalled by the Trump administration’s failure to assure Democrats that the president would lay off his attacks on “ windmills ” and other clean energy projects

But in recent days, lawmakers appear to have come close to a fragile détente on the back of a “ very reasonable opening proposal ” from the White House, according to Senator Sheldon Whitehouse, a Democrat from Rhode Island and ranking member of the Environment and Public Works Committee.  If the BAAJA is passed, it will codify new protections that legally prevent presidents like Trump from meddling with already-permitted energy projects or singling out specific forms of energy, a prohibition that will also apply if a Democratic president attempts to halt an approved gas line or a petroleum refinery
The Biden administration’s freeze on approvals for new natural gas export plants , for example, would not be allowed.  It’s this element of the proposed bill that worries many environmentalists most

According to a transcript obtained by Punchbowl News, during a coalition call on Thursday, dozens of advocates from prominent environmental groups — including the Sierra Club, the National Wildlife Federation, and the Environmental Law & Policy Center — expressed their misgivings about the bill and strategized about how to lobby Democrats against it
Most environmentalists acknowledge, however, that we need to spruce up the power grid and fix how permitting works for clean energy projects and transmission lines

As clean energy advocates know all too well, the projects they support are, paradoxically, more likely to be hampered by environmental reviews than fossil fuel projects are, because renewables usually require more space and represent the bulk of new energy developments

But many advocates understandably take issue with the idea that reforming this overcomplicated process may require weakening the right to challenge other projects, a right affirmed by the National Environmental Policy Act, the Clean Water Act, the Endangered Species Act, and the National Historic Preservation Act.  The bill’s fate may ultimately depend on whether this trade-off is worth it
The BAAJA still does leave some room for court challenges if they’re filed within 150 days of an approval

But it will still place a much larger burden for determining these damage thresholds on federal agencies, which are, of course, currently controlled by Trump. “The question’s not whether that would be a good idea — it’s one of the basic building blocks for converting more of our energy system to renewables,” the environmentalist Bill McKibben wrote of grid expansion and permitting reform on his Substack this week. “It’s how many pounds of flesh the fossil fuel industry would demand in return, and how close to vital organs that flesh would be located.” The problem is, no matter how many Congressional seats Democrats seem poised to scoop up in November, they will still need to get Republicans on board if they want Americans to be able to really see the benefits of solar, the cheapest energy source of all time , reflected on their power bill
And for most of the nation, if not Earth itself, that transition can’t come soon enough.

title: Gen Z is warming to socialism. But they’re still not sure what it means.
excerpt: Zohran Mamdani, then-New York City mayoral candidate, and Letitia James, far left, New York's attorney general, carry a banner across the Brooklyn Bridge in New
body: Zohran Mamdani, then-New York City mayoral candidate, and Letitia James, far left, New York's attorney general, carry a banner across the Brooklyn Bridge in New York on November 3, 2025. | Adam Gray/Bloomberg via Getty Images Socialism is breaking through to the mainstream this year, with surveys showing most Democrats, and plenty of independents, now view the term positively.  The shift is being led by young people in particular, who have also helped left-populist candidates win high-stakes primaries this year
A Cato Institute poll from June found that over half of Gen Z are more supportive of socialism (53 percent) than capitalism (45 percent)

And more than half (57 percent) of people ages 18 to 34 have a positive view of socialism, according to a Gallup poll from August — versus just 34 percent of people over 55.  Figures like these are inspiring socialist organizers and frightening Republicans , who are accusing Democrats of sliding into “communism” in their midterm messaging
But here’s a little secret I’ve been hearing in the focus groups I run through my research, media, and strategy company focused on Gen Z — it’s not “socialism” that’s attractive to young voters

In fact, there’s little agreement on what the word really means.  Instead, it’s the social policies these candidates are running on that resonate — things like affordable housing, healthcare, education, a higher minimum wage, and higher taxes on corporations and wealthy individuals
All summer long, I asked Gen Z voters to define socialism

There was no consensus answer, but much less talk of “workers controlling the means of production,” as one 22-year-old woman from New Jersey referenced, and much more of a focus on what a 21-year-old man from Florida described as a “social safety net.”  Understanding where they’re coming from is important to both critics and supporters: Revolutionaries and reactionaries alike who think young people are signing up for a specific ideology are misreading the moment

When it comes to the rise of “socialism,” young people want what they’ve always wanted: to be heard, and to be helped.   Why socialism is resonating with Gen Z Gen Z’s interest in the term was closely tied to the myriad ways their economic outlook has deteriorated in the past year.  “I feel like over the last year things definitely have changed

You see it generally even with gas prices. … A lot of it has to do with the fact that our country has involved itself in a lot of different conflicts around the world at this point,” the 21-year-old from Florida said.  “During the school year I am relying on my refunds from school to pay my rent, to pay my car payment and car insurance, phone bill, internet, stuff like that,” said another 21-year-old man from Pennsylvania.  “I haven’t been able to financially plan for my education in the way I thought I was going to and have been needing to save more of my own money from jobs I’m working to help account for those differences,” said a 21-year-old woman from North Carolina.  As economic anxiety reshapes Gen Z’s politics and life feels harder and harder to afford, young people are looking for the government to provide social support.  Consistently, I asked groups of young people this summer what they’re looking for in an ideal political candidate — and the government more broadly

Overwhelmingly, they told me they’re in favor of politicians who understand everyday people and a government that provides social services for its constituents. “A political candidate who understands the common person
Someone that’s not financially out of touch, who doesn’t take money from different corporations

Someone who understands the struggles of an everyday American and knows what’s going on with the economy and can understand the struggles of students, children, families,” said a 21-year-old woman from Michigan. “Providing a higher safety net with welfare, especially with hospitals because of the ‘big, beautiful bill’ and its effects,” said a 19-year-old from New York City, citing the impact of the Trump administration’s recent tax bill that slashed healthcare spending . “A candidate who isn’t afraid to say that we deserve more as citizens,” said another 19-year-old woman from Michigan.   According to many of the young voters I spoke to, in their eyes, this is what socialism means: a more ambitious, generous, and equality-minded government

And when I asked them to tell me about the policies they associate with democratic socialists, they said things like “Medicare-for-all,” “help with college tuition,” and “social safety nets like healthcare, public education, public housing.”  Where young people see socialism working In pushing back against socialism’s rising popularity, critics often invoke history, pointing to Marxist governments where equality was instituted by force and coercion and associated with poverty and deprivation.  “They’ve gone communist, but we’re not going to let that happen,” President Donald Trump said at a South Carolina rally in August . “It’s never worked in 1,000 years with different names, lots of different names
It’s never worked once.” Just as Gen Z was presumed to be “woke” Democrats four years ago and then swung hard to Trump and MAGA in 2024, the socialist turn is just as conditional
On the whole, however, young people I spoke to were less likely to tie socialism to “communism” or to places like Cuba, Venezuela, or Soviet Russia

Instead, they gave examples where they perceive socialism to work well, often mentioning wealthy Western countries and the social support systems associated with these kinds of governments.   “I think Scandinavian countries and those countries have had socialist policies in place and people end up having universal healthcare and people are able to live more comfortably and receive more money from the government to support them,” said a 21-year-old woman from Massachusetts. “I know in Canada there’s some socialist policies that I think have benefited people in regards to healthcare and welfare and social security.”  This shouldn’t be surprising

With years of distance from the Marxist governments that our parents and grandparents may think back to (even the oldest Gen Z were born well after the Cold War ended) young people are more focused on social policies than the core tenets of socialism.  “The first thing that comes to mind is the government’s involvement in making sure that everybody is cared for and everyone’s health remains a priority despite their income,” said that 21-year-old woman from Massachusetts. “And I think that is something that makes me view socialism in more of a positive light because some people obviously don’t have the same financial situations as others

That doesn’t mean that they should be undervalued in society.” Liking socialism doesn’t mean identifying as a socialist But just as socialism’s detractors are misunderstanding its appeal among young voters, its supporters should be just as wary of assuming voters are signing up for their movement.  I’ve heard anecdotes like the ones above shared over and over again
And yet, very few young people I’ve spoken to in the past few months have been willing to call themselves a socialist
This is consistent with a broader Gen Z skepticism toward political parties

While they’re leaning into the policies associated with “socialism,” they still largely reject labels — whether that label is Republican, Democrat, or…socialist.  Asked if she would consider herself a democratic socialist or a socialist, the 21-year-old from Massachusetts said she “would definitely lean that way.” A 19-year-old woman from Colorado said, “I would say I lean towards it, but I haven’t completely been with that party.”  And a 23-year-old woman from Arizona said: “I would say I’m in between democrat and democratic socialist.”  And while a 19-year-old from Michigan said she appreciates that democratic socialists are “going to help get baseline needs for people across America met in ways that aren’t going to happen if we have someone who is taking money from PACs and corporations making money off of people going into medical debt and things like that,” but asked if she would label herself that way, she said, “I feel like I don’t know enough about it.” This isn’t universal
Polls suggest a sizable number of young Democrats identify as democratic socialist when asked

But when it comes to organized political behavior, the Democratic Socialists of America only recently passed 120,000 official members , even as they’ve had unprecedented success in raising their profile and nominating candidates this cycle
Just as Gen Z was presumed to be “woke” Democrats four years ago and then swung hard to Trump and MAGA in 2024, the socialist turn is just as conditional
They’re looking for concrete solutions, not dogma, and if they don’t see results, they’ll look elsewhere.

title: Redefining enterprise intelligence with autonomous AI
excerpt: Enterprise AI is no longer a future ambition
body: Enterprise AI is no longer a future ambition
Model capabilities are advancing faster than most organizations can absorb, while the cost of performance continues to fall
Globally, AI investment is set to reach $2.5 trillion in 2026, up 44% from the previous year
For many enterprises, this investment has produced fragmentation

Intelligence can accumulate in silos so that sales agents are unaware of open support tickets, for instance, or marketing systems are personalizing content without visibility into what finance already knows about a customer
Each function may perform well in isolation, but the enterprise as a whole learns little and has less information to act upon

DOWNLOAD THE REPORT The shift from AI as a tool to AI as an operating model—what we call the “agentic shift” in this report—demands something more fundamental than better models or faster infrastructure
It requires connecting people, processes, and data in real time, along with the governance and control to act on that intelligence reliably
This means rethinking both architecture and operating models simultaneously
First, rebuilding data infrastructure for accessibility rather than volume
Second, replacing fixed tech stacks with composable architectures that can evolve as models and tools change
And, lastly, resolving questions of AI sovereignty, including where intelligence runs, who controls it, and how it operates across organizational and jurisdictional boundaries
Key findings include the following: Enterprise AI’s scaling problem is structural
Process-first companies are pulling ahead
Global AI spending is rising sharply and model capabilities are advancing faster than most organizations can integrate them
Yet the majority of enterprises are still not growing revenue through AI or fundamentally rethinking how they operate
The companies generating sustained returns share a common discipline
They treat process redesign as the work that precedes model selection, building for how the technology will evolve rather than retrofitting roles and workflows after deployment
For them, the agentic shift begins with the operating model
Data readiness, not data abundance, is what makes AI compoundable
Most enterprises discover too late that having data and having AI-ready data are very different things
A sovereign, composable foundation—one that queries and prepares data where it resides, without migration or centralization—can convert raw data estates into intelligence that AI agents can act upon

As data residency laws, multicloud environments, and structural complexity make centralization increasingly impractical, sovereign control over where models run and data lives is what keeps that adaptability intact
